33	## 1. V&V Fundamentals
34	
35	### Core Definitions
36	
37	> [!warning] Most Examined Distinction
38	> These two questions are **always** the starting point of any exam question on V&V.
39	
40	| Term | Question | Focus |
41	|------|----------|-------|
42	| **Verification** | "Are we building the product **right**?" | Conformance to specification |
43	| **Validation** | "Are we building the **right** product?" | Fulfilment of user needs and intended purpose |
44	| **V&V combined** | "Does it meet specs **and** fulfil its purpose?" | Both simultaneously |
45	
46	### Static vs Dynamic V&V
47	
48	| | **Static V&V** | **Dynamic V&V** |
49	|---|---|---|
50	| Code executed? | **No** | **Yes** |
51	| Focus | **Prevention** of defects | **Detection** of defects |
52	| Methods | Reviews, inspections, walkthroughs, SAST tools | Testing, simulation, model checking |

56	### The V-Model

60	    R["📋 Requirements"] -.->|validates| AT["✅ Acceptance\nTesting"]

106	## 2. Testing Fundamentals
107	
108	### The Seven ISTQB Principles
109	
110	> [!note] Mnemonic: **T**each **E**very **E**ager **D**eveloper **P**roper **T**esting **A**pproaches
111	
112	| # | Principle | One-Line Meaning |
113	|---|-----------|-----------------|
114	| 1 | **Testing shows presence of defects** | Proves defects exist; cannot prove zero defects |
115	| 2 | **Exhaustive testing is impossible** | Use risk analysis to focus effort |
116	| 3 | **Early testing saves cost** | Shift left — find defects before they embed |
117	| 4 | **Defect clustering** | 80% of defects live in ~20% of the code (Pareto) |
118	| 5 | **Pesticide paradox** | Repeated identical tests stop finding new defects — refresh suites |
119	| 6 | **Testing is context-dependent** | Safety-critical ≠ marketing website |
120	| 7 | **Absence-of-errors fallacy** | Zero defects ≠ useful software; must test the right things |
121	
122	### Error → Defect → Failure Chain
123	
124	```mermaid
125	flowchart LR
126	    E["💭 Error / Mistake\nHuman action\ne.g. developer\nmisunderstands req"] -->|creates| D["🐛 Fault / Bug / Defect\nFlaw in code\ne.g. wrong condition\nin if-statement"]
127	    D -->|when executed| F["💥 Failure\nDeviation from\nexpected behaviour\nvisible to user"]
128	    style E fill:#fff3e0,color:#000
129	    style D fill:#ffccbc,color:#000
130	    style F fill:#f44336,color:#fff
131	```
132	
133	> "Testing can show that defects are present, but cannot prove there are no defects." — Bill Hetzel
134	
135	### Four Testing Levels
136	
137	```
138	┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
139	│           Acceptance Testing (UAT)                    │
140	│  "Are we building the RIGHT product?"                 │
141	│  Techniques: Use cases, real user scenarios           │
142	├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
143	│              System Testing                           │
144	│  "Does the complete system work?"                     │
145	│  Techniques: Blackbox — EP, BVA, Decision Tables      │
146	├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
147	│           Integration Testing                         │
148	│  "Do the components work together?"                   │
149	│  Techniques: Mix of blackbox / whitebox               │
150	├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
151	│              Unit Testing                             │
152	│  "Does each isolated unit work correctly?"            │
153	│  Techniques: Whitebox — CFG, coverage criteria        │
154	└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
155	```
156	
157	### The Testing Pyramid
158	
159	```
160	           ▲
161	          /E2E\         ← Few; slow; expensive; flaky
162	         /──────\
163	        /Integration\   ← Some; moderately fast
164	       /──────────────\
165	      /  Unit Tests    \ ← Many; fast; cheap; high ROI
166	     /──────────────────\
167	
168	Recommended distribution: 70% Unit — 20% Integration — 10% E2E
169	```
170	
171	> [!warning] Anti-Pattern: Ice Cream Cone
172	> Many teams invert the pyramid — heavy reliance on manual/UI tests, few unit tests. Result: slow CI, brittle tests, high maintenance cost. Fix: push tests **down** the pyramid.
173	
174	### Static Testing Techniques (Formality Spectrum)
175	
176	```mermaid
177	flowchart LR
178	    A["Informal\nReview\n(lowest formality)"] --> B["Walkthrough\n(author-led)"]
179	    B --> C["Technical\nReview\n(moderator-led)"]
180	    C --> D["Inspection\n(Fagan — highest\nformality, most\ncost-effective)"]
181	    style D fill:#c8e6c9,color:#000
182	```
183	
184	| Technique | Who leads | Output | Formality |
185	|-----------|-----------|--------|-----------|
186	| Informal review | Author | None required | Lowest |
187	| Walkthrough | Author | Issues noted | Low |
188	| Technical review | Moderator | Defect list | Medium |
189	| **Inspection (Fagan)** | Trained moderator | Metrics + formal report | **Highest / Most cost-effective** |
190	
191	### Retesting vs Regression Testing
192	
193	| Type | Definition |
194	|------|-----------|
195	| **Retesting** | Re-running tests that **previously found defects** to confirm the fix works |
196	| **Regression testing** | Running tests in **parallel areas** to confirm fixes don't break something else |
197	
198	> [!warning] Up to 50% of bug fixes introduce additional errors. Regression testing is not optional.
199	
200	### Eight Good Testing Practices
201	
202	| # | Practice |
203	|---|---------|
204	| 1 | A good test has **high probability of detecting undiscovered defects** — not just showing it works |
205	| 2 | Don't be the **only one testing your own code** — peer review is essential |
206	| 3 | Specify **expected result before** running the test |
207	| 4 | Write tests for both **valid and invalid** inputs |
208	| 5 | **Thoroughly inspect results** of each test |
209	| 6 | Make **testability** a key design objective |
210	| 7 | **Never alter the programme** to make testing easier |
211	| 8 | Testing must start with clear **objectives** |
212	
213	### Goodhart's Law in Testing
214	
215	> "When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure."
216	
217	**Applied:** When teams are evaluated on test counts or coverage %, they write tests designed to pass rather than to find defects. The goal is **finding defects**, not achieving metric targets.
218

221	## 3. Software Reliability Metrics
222	
223	### Core Metrics
224	
225	| Metric | Formula | Meaning |
226	|--------|---------|---------|
227	| **MTTF** | Empirical | Mean Time To Failure — avg time from start to first failure |
228	| **MTTR** | Empirical | Mean Time To Repair — avg time to restore after failure |
229	| **MTBF** | MTTF + MTTR | Mean Time Between Failures |
230	| **Availability** | MTTF / (MTTF + MTTR) | Proportion of time system is operational |
231	
232	> [!example] Worked Example
233	> MTTF = 9 hours, MTTR = 1 hour
234	> MTBF = 9 + 1 = **10 hours**
235	> Availability = 9 / 10 = **0.9 = 90%**
236	
237	> [!warning] Lab simplification
238	> The lab uses `MTBF / (MTBF + MTTR)` (substituting MTBF for MTTF). Know both forms.
239	
240	### Execution Time vs Calendar Time
241	
242	| Type | Also Called | Definition | Differs when… |
243	|------|------------|-----------|--------------|
244	| **Execution time** | CPU time | Cumulative processor time consumed | Multi-threaded: many CPU-s fit in fewer wall-clock seconds |
245	| **Calendar time** | Wall-clock time | Real-world elapsed time | I/O-bound: CPU idles; wall time > CPU time |
246	
247	> Always specify environment when reporting time-based metrics.
248	
249	### Basic Musa Reliability Model
250	
251	Assumes **constant rate of decrease** in failure intensity — each fault fixed reduces failure rate by the same amount.
252	
253	$$\mu(\tau) = \nu_0 \times \left[1 - e^{-\lambda_0 \tau / \nu_0}\right]$$
254	
255	$$\lambda(\tau) = \lambda_0 \times e^{-\lambda_0 \tau / \nu_0}$$
256	
257	| Symbol | Meaning |
258	|--------|---------|
259	| μ(τ) | Expected total failures by time τ |
260	| λ(τ) | Failure intensity at time τ |
261	| ν₀ | Total expected failures (initial fault count) |
262	| λ₀ | Initial failure intensity |
263	
264	**Suited for:** stable/mature releases where faults are evenly distributed.
265	
266	> [!example] Worked Check (λ₀=2, ν₀=10, τ=5)
267	> Exponent = −λ₀τ/ν₀ = −(2×5)/10 = −1
268	> λ(5) = 2 × e⁻¹ ≈ **0.7358 failures/time unit**
269	> μ(5) = 10 × (1 − e⁻¹) ≈ **6.3212 expected failures**
270	
271	### Logarithmic Musa Reliability Model
272	
273	Assumes frequently-triggered faults are found first — **diminishing returns** as testing continues.
274	
275	$$\mu(\tau) = \frac{1}{\theta} \ln(\lambda_0 \theta \tau + 1)$$
276	
277	$$\lambda(\tau) = \lambda_0 \times e^{-\theta \mu(\tau)}$$
278	
279	| Symbol | Meaning |
280	|--------|---------|
281	| θ | Per-fault decrease in intensity (higher = more skewed fault distribution) |
282	
283	**Suited for:** early testing where a few heavily-used paths accumulate most failures first. Tends toward zero but never reaches it — arguably more realistic.
284	
285	**Key distinction:** High-traffic bugs surface quickly → large initial drop in λ → diminishing returns for rare paths.
286	
287	### Defect Density
288	
289	$$\text{Defect Density} = \frac{\text{Defects}}{\text{KLOC}}$$
290	
291	- **KLOC** = Kilo Lines of Code (1,000 LOC)
292	- **SSI** = Shipped Source Instructions
293	- **CSI** = Changed Source Instructions
294	
295	**Tracking across releases:**
296	```
297	KSSI(current) = KSSI(previous) + KCSI − deleted_lines − changed_lines
298	```
299	
300	### Customer-Facing Metrics
301	
302	**PUM — Problems per User Month:**
303	
304	$$\text{PUM} = \frac{\text{Total Problems}}{\text{Total User Months}}$$
305	
306	**Total User Months** = number of users × months in period.
307	
308	**Quality Frameworks:**

310	| Framework | Dimensions |
311	|-----------|-----------|
312	| **IBM CUPRIMDSO** | Capability, Usability, Performance, Reliability, Installability, Maintainability, Documentation, Service, Overall |
313	| **HP FURPS** | Functionality, Usability, Reliability, Performance, Supportability |
314	
315	---
316	
317	## 4. Static Analysis
318	
319	### Why Static Analysis?
320	
321	| Testing | Static Analysis |
322	|---------|----------------|
323	| Finds bugs on exercised paths only | Reasons about **all paths simultaneously** |
324	| Cannot cover rare paths | Finds bugs in untested paths |
325	| Cannot detect race conditions reliably | Can model concurrent execution states |
326	
327	### Data Flow Defect Classes
328	
329	```mermaid
330	flowchart LR
331	    D1["Use Before Define\nVariable accessed\nbefore assignment"]
332	    D2["Define, Never Used\nAssigned but\nnever read"]
333	    D3["Destroy Then Use\nFreed/nulled\nthen accessed"]
334	    D4["Redefine\nWithout Use\nNew value assigned\nbefore old consumed"]
335	    style D1 fill:#ffccbc,color:#000
336	    style D2 fill:#ffccbc,color:#000
337	    style D3 fill:#f44336,color:#fff
338	    style D4 fill:#ffccbc,color:#000
339	```
340	
341	> [!tip] Modern IDEs flag many of these automatically (e.g., "variable used before assignment"). Understanding the underlying classes matters for code inspection and exam questions.
342	
343	### When Static Analysis Runs
344	
345	| Timing | Examples |
346	|--------|---------|
347	| Before compile-time | IDE warnings, lint checks |
348	| At compile-time | Type checking, compiler warnings (`-Wall`) |
349	| After compile-time | SAST tools in CI/CD pipeline |
350	
351	---
352	
353	## 5. Whitebox Testing
354	
355	> **"Tests derived from the internal structure of the code."** Applied primarily at unit and integration testing levels.
356	
357	### Two Categories
358	
359	| Category | Purpose |
360	|----------|---------|
361	| **Control Flow** | Identify execution paths; design test cases to cover those paths |
362	| **Data Flow** | Identify improper use of data values due to coding errors |
363	
364	---
365	
366	### Control Flow Graphs (CFGs)
367	
368	A CFG is a directed graph where:
369	- **Nodes** = statements or statement blocks
370	- **Edges** = transitions between statements
371	
372	#### Node Types
373	
374	| Type | Description | Diagram |
375	|------|------------|---------|
376	| **Sequence** | Linear statements | → A → B → |
377	| **If-then-else** | Binary decision | → D → T or F |
378	| **Case/Switch** | Multiple exits | → D → C1, C2, C3 |
379	| **Junction** | Paths converge | T, F → → |
380	| **While loop** | Condition before body | back-edge when true |
381	| **Do-until** | Body before condition | executes at least once |
382	
383	#### Reference Example — Factorial
384	
385	```
386	int i=1, facto=1          ← node 1
387	input num                 ← node 2
388	if (num < 0)              ← node 3 (DECISION)
389	  print "nope"            ← node 4
390	else
391	  while (i <= num)        ← node 6 (DECISION — back-edge from 9)
392	    facto = facto * i     ← node 7
393	    i++                   ← node 8
394	  end-while               ← node 9 → back to 6
395	  print(facto)            ← node 10
396	end-if                    ← node 11
397	```
398	
399	```mermaid
400	flowchart TD
401	    N1["1: i=1, facto=1"] --> N2["2: input num"]
402	    N2 --> N3{"3: num < 0?"}
403	    N3 -->|True| N4["4: print 'nope'"]
404	    N3 -->|False| N6{"6: i <= num?"}
405	    N4 --> N11["11: end"]
406	    N6 -->|False| N10["10: print facto"]
407	    N6 -->|True| N7["7: facto = facto × i"]
408	    N7 --> N8["8: i++"]
409	    N8 --> N9["9: end-while"] --> N6
410	    N10 --> N11
411	    style N3 fill:#ffe0b2,color:#000
412	    style N6 fill:#ffe0b2,color:#000
413	```
414	
415	**CFG Stats:** 11 nodes, 12 edges (including back-edge 9→6)
416	**Three paths:**
417	
418	| Path | Node Sequence | Trigger |
419	|------|--------------|---------|
420	| **P1** | 1→2→3→4→11 | num < 0 |
421	| **P2** | 1→2→3→6→10→11 | num = 0 (loop skipped) |
422	| **P3** | 1→2→3→6→7→8→9→6→10→11 | num > 0 (loop runs) |
423	
424	---
425	
426	### Coverage Criteria — Hierarchy
427	
428	```mermaid
429	flowchart TD
430	    PC["Path Coverage\n(impractical for loops)"]
431	    MCC["Multiple Condition\nCoverage\n2ⁿ test cases"]
432	    DCC["Decision & Condition\nCoverage"]
433	    CC["Condition Coverage\n⚠️ does NOT subsume Decision"]
434	    DC["Decision/Branch\nCoverage\nsubsumes Statement"]
435	    SC["Statement Coverage\n(weakest baseline)"]
436	    PC --> MCC --> DCC
437	    DCC --> CC
438	    DCC --> DC --> SC
439	    style CC fill:#fff3e0,color:#000
440	    style MCC fill:#c8e6c9,color:#000
441	    style PC fill:#e8f5e9,color:#000
442	```
443	
444	---
445	
446	### Coverage Criteria — Detail
447	
448	#### 1. Statement Coverage (Weakest)
449	
450	> Every executable statement executed at least once.
451	
452	$$\text{Coverage \%} = \frac{\text{statements executed}}{\text{total executable statements}} \times 100$$
453	
454	**Factorial:** 2 test cases (num > 0, num < 0) cover all 11 nodes.
455	
456	---
457	
458	#### 2. Decision / Branch Coverage
459	
460	> Every decision's **True** and **False** outcomes each executed at least once. **Subsumes** statement coverage.
461	
462	$$\text{Coverage \%} = \frac{\text{decision outcomes executed}}{\text{total decision outcomes}} \times 100$$
463	
464	**Factorial:** 2 decisions (`if`, `while`) × 2 outcomes = 4 outcomes needed.
465	- Path 1 (num < 0): if→True ✓, while→False ✓
466	- Path 2 (num > 0): if→False ✓, while→True ✓ (False covered when loop ends)
467	
468	---
469	
470	#### 3. Condition Coverage
471	
472	> Each **individual sub-condition** within a compound decision takes both True and False at least once.
473	
474	> [!warning] Critical Gap — Condition coverage does NOT subsume Decision coverage!
475	
476	```
477	if (X and Y):
478	    print("tested")
479	```
480	
481	| TC | X | Y | Conditions Covered | Branch Taken |
482	|----|---|---|--------------------|-------------|
483	| 1 | T | F | X=T ✓, Y=F ✓ | False only |
484	| 2 | F | T | X=F ✓, Y=T ✓ | False only |
485	
486	100% condition coverage achieved — but the **True branch is NEVER executed!**
487	
488	---
489	
490	#### 4. Decision & Condition Coverage
491	
492	> Both Condition coverage and Decision coverage satisfied simultaneously — closes the gap above.
493	
494	---
495	
496	#### 5. Multiple Condition Coverage
497	
498	> All possible T/F **combinations** of each condition group are exercised.
499	
500	For `if (A && B && C)`: 2³ = **8 test cases** required. Subsumes all lower criteria.
501	
502	---
503	
504	#### 6. Path Coverage + Loop Coverage
505	
506	> Every distinct control flow path exercised. Impractical for loops → use Loop Coverage:
507	
508	| Iteration | Description |
509	|-----------|------------|
510	| **Zero** | Loop body never executes (skip condition) |
511	| **One** | Loop executes exactly once |
512	| **Typical** | Normal number of iterations |
513	| **Max** | Maximum feasible iterations |
514	
515	---
516	
517	### Coverage Summary Table
518	
519	| Criterion | Subsumes | Min TCs (Factorial) | Use Case |
520	|-----------|----------|---------------------|---------|
521	| Statement | — | 2 | Minimum baseline |
522	| Decision/Branch | Statement | 2 | Standard CI target |
523	| Condition | ⚠️ Neither subsumes Decision | 2+ | Compound conditions |
524	| D & C | Decision + Condition | 2+ | Better practice |
525	| Multiple Condition | All above | 2ⁿ per group | Safety-critical |
526	| Path (+ loop) | Multiple Condition | 3+ | Safety-critical only |
527	
528	---
529	
530	### Cyclomatic Complexity (McCabe, 1976)
531	
532	$$\boxed{C = E - N + 2}$$
533	
534	- **E** = edges in the CFG
535	- **N** = nodes in the CFG
536	- **C** = minimum number of **independent basis paths**
537	
538	**Factorial:** C = 12 − 11 + 2 = **3**
539	
540	#### Threshold Values
541	
542	| C Range | Risk |
543	|---------|------|
544	| 1–4 | Simple, low risk |
545	| 5–10 | Marginal, low risk |
546	| 11–20 | Complex, moderate risk |
547	| 21–50 | Complex, **high risk** |
548	| > 50 | **Untestable**, very high risk |
549	
550	---
551	
552	### Basis Path Testing
553	
554	**Basis paths** = independent, non-looping paths that can linearly generate all other paths through a module.
555	
556	**Independent path:** introduces at least one new statement or edge not seen in previous paths.
557	
558	**Five-step process:**
559	
560	```mermaid
561	flowchart LR
562	    A["1. Model code\nas CFG"] --> B["2. Compute C\n= E − N + 2"]
563	    B --> C["3. Select C\nbasis paths\n(each adds new edge)"]
564	    C --> D["4. Create test\ncase per path"]
565	    D --> E["5. Execute\nand verify"]
566	```
567	
568	**Guarantee:** Basis path testing guarantees **at least full branch coverage**.
569	
570	**Factorial (C = 3):**
571	
572	| Path # | Input | Expected Output |
573	|--------|-------|----------------|
574	| 1 | num = −1 | "nope" |
575	| 2 | num = 0 | 1 |
576	| 3 | num = 3 | 6 |
577	
578	---
579	
580	### LCSAJ — Linear Code Sequence and Jump
581	
582	LCSAJ breaks code into **tuples (X, Y, Z)**:
583	- **X** = first statement of the linear sequence
584	- **Y** = last statement (where the jump occurs)
585	- **Z** = jump target (another statement or `exit`)
586	
587	**LCSAJ provides 100% decision coverage.**
588	
589	> [!example] Simple If-Else Example
590	> ```
591	> 1. // begin
592	> 2. int num
593	> 3. input(num)
594	> 4. if (num < 0)
595	> 5.   print "less"
596	> 6. else
597	> 7.   print "more"
598	> 8. // end
599	> ```
600	>
601	> | Tuple | (X, Y, Z) | Traversed by |
602	> |-------|-----------|--------------|
603	> | 1 | (1, 4, 7) | Path 2: num ≥ 0 |
604	> | 2 | (1, 6, exit) | Path 1: num < 0 |
605	> | 3 | (7, 8, exit) | Path 2: num ≥ 0 |
606	>
607	> **Full coverage with 2 test cases** (X = −5 and X = 5).
608	
609	---
610	
611	## 6. Blackbox Testing
612	
613	> **"Tests derived from the specification without reference to the internal structure."** Applied at all levels, most commonly at system and acceptance testing.
614	
615	### Five Techniques Overview
616	
617	| Technique | Best For | Key Strength |
618	|-----------|---------|--------------|
619	| **Use Case Testing** | End-to-end flows; integration defects | Detects real-world usage problems |
620	| **Equivalence Partitioning** | Large input domains | Minimises test cases efficiently |
621	| **Boundary Value Analysis** | Ranged inputs | High defect yield at boundaries |
622	| **Decision Table Testing** | Multi-condition logic | Exhaustive condition combinations |
623	| **State Transition Testing** | FSMs, protocols, UIs | Exposes missing/dead/unspecified states |
624	
625	---
626	
627	### 1. Use Case Testing
628	
629	Tests the system from the **user's perspective** — not the developer's.
630	
631	#### Use Case Components
632	
633	| Component | Description |
634	|-----------|------------|
635	| **Actors** | Users or external systems interacting |
636	| **Preconditions** | Must hold before execution |
637	| **Postconditions** | System state after execution |
638	| **Primary system flow** | Happy-path sequence |
639	| **Alternative flows** | Errors, exceptions, alternate paths |
640	
641	#### What Scenario Tests Detect
642	
643	1. Defects from **real-world usage** patterns
644	2. **Integration defects** at component boundaries
645	3. **Dead-end states** — states the system can enter but cannot exit
646	4. Defects invisible in isolated unit tests
647	
648	> [!example] Resource Loan System
649	> - TC#1: Valid loan (MSP430, ID:001) → grants eligibility, displays to PO
650	> - TC#2: Invalid item (Chemical X) → fails eligibility, shows error
651	
652	---
653	
654	### 2. Equivalence Partitioning (EP)
655	
656	**Goal:** Minimise test cases while maintaining broad coverage.
657	
658	**Mechanism:** Divide input domain into groups where every value in a group produces the same result. Test **one representative per partition**.
659	
660	#### Example — Integer Input 0–100
661	
662	```
663	◄─────────────────────────────────────────►
664	   Invalid 1    |      Valid       | Invalid 2
665	    x < 0       |   0 ≤ x ≤ 100   |  x > 100
666	─────────────────────────────────────────────
667	   e.g. −10           e.g. 50        e.g. 110
668	```
669	
670	**Minimum test set:** 3 test cases (one per partition).
671	
672	#### EP Advantages / Disadvantages
673	
674	| ✅ Advantages | ❌ Disadvantages |
675	|---|---|
676	| Easy to analyse | Excludes some inputs |
677	| Applicable at all test levels | No rule for selecting value within a partition |
678	| Minimises test cases | No guarantee all elements behave identically |
679	| Can partition both inputs **and outputs** | Limited focus on input combinations |
680	
681	---
682	
683	### 3. Boundary Value Analysis (BVA)
684	
685	**Goal:** Design tests specifically at **boundary values** — defects cluster at the edges of ranges.
686	
687	**Complements EP:** while EP selects one value per partition, BVA selects values **at and just beyond** each boundary.
688	
689	#### Example — Integer 0–100
690	
691	```
692	──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
693	   Invalid │ Valid Lower │    Valid Interior    │ Valid Upper │ Invalid
694	           │             │                     │             │
695	          -1      0       1          99        100     101
696	                  ↑                             ↑
697	             Lower valid                    Upper valid
698	             boundary                      boundary
699	```
700	
701	| Value | Type |
702	|-------|------|
703	| −1 | Invalid lower boundary (just below) |
704	| 0 | Valid lower boundary |
705	| 1 | Low + 1 (extended BVA) |
706	| 99 | High − 1 (extended BVA) |
707	| 100 | Valid upper boundary |
708	| 101 | Invalid upper boundary (just above) |
709	
710	#### Example — String: First Name (1–10 Capital Letters A–Z)
711	
712	| Test Value | Type | Boundary |
713	|-----------|------|---------|
714	| "G" (1 char) | Valid | Lower length |
715	| "A" (ASCII 65) | Valid | Lower ASCII |
716	| "BORDERNAME" (10 chars) | Valid | Upper length |
717	| "Z" (ASCII 90) | Valid | Upper ASCII |
718	| null / empty | Invalid | Null boundary |
719	| "@" (ASCII 64) | Invalid | Just below 'A' |
720	| "FAKEBIGNAME" (11 chars) | Invalid | Just above upper length |
721	| "[" (ASCII 91) | Invalid | Just above 'Z' |
722	
723	> [!warning] Test ASCII boundary and string length boundary in **separate test cases**. Combining them obscures which boundary caused the failure.
724	
725	#### Four General BVA Rules
726	
727	| Rule | Guidance |
728	|------|---------|
729	| **1** | Range of values → valid tests at each end; invalid tests just beyond each end. Consider output conditions too. |
730	| **2** | No specified range → use min and max values plus one below and one above. |
731	| **3** | Sets of values → test each value and set size; for files test first and last records. |
732	| **4** | Any extreme input or output → test it. |
733	
734	---
735	
736	### 4. Decision Table Testing
737	
738	**Goal:** Model complex logic precisely — every combination of conditions mapped to actions.
739	
740	**Structure:** Each **column (Rule)** = unique combination of condition values → specific set of actions.
741	
742	$$n \text{ binary conditions} \Rightarrow \text{maximum } 2^n \text{ rules}$$
743	
744	#### Example 1 — Movie Ticket Pricing
745	
746	| Condition | Rule 1 | Rule 2 | Rule 3 | Rule 4 |
747	|-----------|--------|--------|--------|--------|
748	| Student? | Yes | Yes | No | No |
749	| Aged < 21? | Yes | No | Yes | No |
750	| **Discount** | **15%** | **10%** | **5%** | **None** |
751	
752	**Test:** one test case per column.
753	
754	#### Example 2 — Movie Ticket System
755	
756	| Condition | Rule 1 | Rule 2 | Rule 3 |
757	|-----------|--------|--------|--------|
758	| Movie ID valid? | N | Y | Y |
759	| Payment valid? | — | N | Y |
760	| Show welcome screen | Y | N | N |
761	| Reject payment | N | Y | N |
762	| Supply ticket | N | N | Y |
763	
764	#### Decision Table Constraints
765	
766	1. Condition evaluation order does not affect the resulting action
767	2. Rule evaluation order does not affect the resulting action
768	3. Once a rule fires, no further rules are examined
769	4. Multiple actions from one rule: action order is ignored
770	5. n binary decisions → 2ⁿ maximum cases
771	6. Find inputs that force **each column (rule)** to execute
772	
773	---
774	
775	### 5. State Transition Testing
776	
777	**Goal:** Design test cases that exercise valid and invalid state transitions in systems with explicit states.
778	
779	#### Applications
780	
781	- Communication protocols (human-machine, system-system, module-module)
782	- User transaction flows with persistent sessions
783	- OS control functions (security handling, permission states)
784	
785	#### Components
786	
787	| Component | Definition |
788	|-----------|-----------|
789	| **State** | Unique system situation defined by variables with specific values; has a duration |
790	| **Transition** | System changes state in response to an input/event |
791	| **Input/Event** | Causes a transition (considered instantaneous) |
792	| **Output/Action** | Associated with each input+transition combination |
793	
794	#### Before Testing — Identify:
795	
796	```mermaid
797	flowchart LR
798	    A["Map system as\nstate diagram"] --> B["Find UNSPECIFIED\ntransitions\n(input in state with\nno defined response)"]
799	    A --> C["Find UNREACHABLE\nstates\n(no path leads\nto them)"]
800	    A --> D["Find DEAD states\n(no exit\ntransition)"]
801	    style B fill:#ffccbc,color:#000
802	    style C fill:#ffccbc,color:#000
803	    style D fill:#f44336,color:#fff
804	```
805	
806	#### Worked Example — Face Recognition Door Lock
807	
808	**States:** S1 (Wait for Face), S2 (Face Recognised, Door Unlocked), S3 (Wait to Activate System)
809	
810	```mermaid
811	stateDiagram-v2
812	    [*] --> S1
813	    S1: S1: Wait for\nRecognised Face
814	    S2: S2: Face Recognised\nDoor Unlocked
815	    S3: S3: Wait to\nActivate System
816	
817	    S1 --> S1 : FU / DL
818	    S1 --> S2 : FR / UD
819	    S2 --> S3 : DR / SA
820	    S2 --> [*] : SLO / SD&AO (unspecified!)
821	    S3 --> S3 : NFD / SI
822	    S3 --> S1 : FD / SO
823	```
824	
825	**Event legend:** FU=Face Unrecognised, FR=Face Recognised, DR=Door Reclosed, SLO=Set Lock Off, NFD=No Face Detected, FD=Face Detected
826	
827	#### 0-Switch Coverage (All Transitions)
828	
829	One test case per transition:
830	
831	| TC | Start | Input | Expected Output | End |
832	|----|-------|-------|-----------------|-----|
833	| 1 | S1 | FU | DL (Door Locked) | S1 |
834	| 2 | S1 | FR | UD (Unlocked) | S2 |
835	| 3 | S2 | DR | SA (Sensors Activated) | S3 |
836	| 4 | S2 | SLO | SD&AO | **Unspecified** |
837	| 5 | S3 | NFD | SI (System Idle) | S3 |
838	| 6 | S3 | FD | SO (System On) | S1 |
839	
840	**6 test cases** → 0-switch coverage.
841	
842	#### 1-Switch Coverage (Consecutive Transition Pairs)
843	
844	Tests every unique **pair** of consecutive transitions. Self-loops excluded.
845	
846	**10 test cases** → 1-switch coverage.
847	
848	| Coverage | Also Called | TCs | What It Covers |
849	|---------|------------|-----|---------------|
850	| **0-switch** | All-transitions | 6 | Every individual transition once |
851	| **1-switch** | Switch coverage | 10 | Every consecutive pair of transitions |
852	
853	---
854	
855	## 7. Comparing Whitebox vs Blackbox
856	
857	```mermaid
858	flowchart LR
859	    subgraph WB["WHITEBOX (Structure-Based)"]
860	        W1["Control Flow:\nCFG, Coverage Criteria\nCyclomatic Complexity\nBasis Paths, LCSAJ"]
861	        W2["Data Flow:\nDefine/Use analysis\nIDE flagged defects"]
862	    end
863	    subgraph BB["BLACKBOX (Specification-Based)"]
864	        B1["Input-based:\nEquivalence Partitioning\nBoundary Value Analysis"]
865	        B2["Logic-based:\nDecision Tables"]
866	        B3["Scenario/State:\nUse Cases\nState Transition"]
867	    end
868	    WB --- |"Complementary\n— use both"| BB
869	```
870	
871	| Dimension | Whitebox | Blackbox |
872	|-----------|---------|---------|
873	| Test basis | **Internal code structure** | **Specification / requirements** |
874	| Code knowledge needed | Full | None required |
875	| Typical level | Unit, integration | System, acceptance |
876	| Finds | Logic errors, dead code, unreachable paths | Missing functionality, incorrect behaviour |
877	| Also called | Structure-based, code-based | Specification-based, functional |
878	
879	---
880	
881	## 8. Key Formulas Reference Sheet
882	
883	| Formula | Name |
884	|---------|------|
885	| MTBF = MTTF + MTTR | Mean Time Between Failures |
886	| Availability = MTTF / (MTTF + MTTR) | System availability |
887	| λ(τ) = λ₀ × e^(−λ₀τ/ν₀) | Basic Musa failure intensity |
888	| μ(τ) = ν₀ × [1 − e^(−λ₀τ/ν₀)] | Basic Musa expected failures |
889	| C = E − N + 2 | Cyclomatic complexity |
890	| 2ⁿ | Max rules in decision table (n binary conditions) |
891	| Defect Density = Defects / KLOC | Defect rate |
892	| PUM = Total Problems / Total User Months | Problems per User Month |
893	
894	---
895	
896	## 9. Exam Checklist
897	
898	> [!tip] For any whitebox question:
899	> 1. Draw the **CFG** first — nodes and edges
900	> 2. Count E and N → compute **C = E − N + 2**
901	> 3. Identify the **coverage criterion** asked for
902	> 4. List the test paths required (remember: Condition ≠ Decision coverage!)
903	> 5. For basis paths: C independent paths, each introducing at least one new edge
904	
905	> [!tip] For any blackbox question:
906	> 1. **EP first** — identify all valid and invalid partitions
907	> 2. **BVA** — find all boundary values (at, just below, just above each boundary)
908	> 3. **Decision table** — list all conditions → 2ⁿ columns max → identify irrelevant/impossible combos
909	> 4. **State transition** — draw the diagram; find unspecified/unreachable/dead states; 0-switch = one TC per transition
910	
911	> [!warning] Common Mistakes to Avoid
912	> - Confusing **Verification** (right product?) with **Validation** (right way?)
913	> - Stating that condition coverage subsumes decision coverage — **it does not**
914	> - Forgetting the back edge in a CFG loop (it contributes an edge to E)
915	> - Using KLOC for defect density when the question gives LOC (divide by 1000 first)
916	> - Forgetting self-loops are **excluded** from 1-switch coverage count
917	> - Omitting test cases for **invalid partitions** in EP — invalid inputs must also be tested
918	> - Ignoring **output** boundaries in BVA — outputs can also have boundary conditions

128	**Exercise A — Larry the Procrastinator:**
129	
130	| Activity | Type |
131	|----------|------|
132	| Going to washroom, setting up laptop | Wait W |
133	| Working on Lab Part 1 (2 min) | Service S |
134	| Getting distracted | Wait W |
135	| Working on Lab Part 2 (8 min) | Service S |

142	|-------|----------|------|
143	| Queuing before registration | 25 min | W |

163	
164	```
165	Response time distribution (right-skewed):
166	
167	Frequency
168	   ↑
169	   │  █

171	   │  ████

173	   │  ████████░░░░░░░░░░░░░░...

191	
192	| Term | Definition | Example |
193	|------|-----------|---------|
194	| **SLI** — Service Level Indicator | The metric being measured | p99 response time |
195	| **SLO** — Service Level Objective | The target value | p99 < 200 ms |
196	| **SLA** — Service Level Agreement | Formal agreement with consequences for breach | Contract with penalty clauses |

200	When one user request triggers N backend calls:

202	$$P(\text{at least one slow}) = 1 - (1 - 0.01)^N$$
203	
204	At N = 100: P ≈ **63%** — the majority of page loads hit the tail.

208	### Utilisation Law: U = X × S
209	
210	**Derivation (pie-eating analogy):**
211	
212	> 60-minute contest. You eat 5 pies at 10 min each.
213	> Busy time = 5 × 10 = 50 min → U = 50/60 = **83%**
214	> X = 5/60 pies/min; U = X × S = (5/60) × 10 = 50/60 ✓
215	
216	| Given | Find | Formula |
217	|-------|------|---------|
218	| λ, S (stable) | U | U = λ × S |
219	| U, X | S | S = U / X |
220	| S | λ_max | λ_max = 1/S (at U = 1) |
221	
222	> [!warning] λ vs X — Critical Distinction
223	> - Stable system: **X = λ** (every arrival is served) → U = λS is valid
224	> - Overloaded system: **X < λ** (work is queued or dropped) → must use **U = XS** (general law)
225	
226	**MRI Scanner Exercises:**
227	
228	| Q | Given | Find | Working | Answer |
229	|---|-------|------|---------|--------|
230	| 1 | λ = 2/hr, S = 25 min | U | 2 × 25/60 | **83%** |
231	| 2 | U = 60%, λ = 12/hr | S | 0.6 / (12/60) | **3 min** |
232	| 3 | S = 6 min | X_max | 60/6 | **10 patients/hr** |

243	   │                                 /

327	## 4. Queueing Theory Foundation
328	
329	### Key Symbols
330	
331	| Symbol | Name | Definition |
332	|--------|------|-----------|
333	| λ | Arrival rate | Jobs offered per unit time — demand at entrance |
334	| μ | Service rate / capacity | μ = 1/S for a single continuously busy server |
335	| S | Service time | Time the server spends processing one job |
336	| X | Throughput | Jobs completed per unit time — supply at exit |
337	| U | Utilisation | Fraction of time server is busy |
338	| W | Wait time | Time in queue, before service begins |
339	| R | Response time | Total time W + S |
340	| ρ | Traffic intensity | ρ = λ/μ = λ × S |
341	| N | Number in system | Average jobs in the system (queue + in service) |
342	
343	### Little's Law
344	
345	$$N = X \times R$$
346	
347	"The average number of items in a system equals the throughput times the average time each item spends in the system."
348	
349	- Applies to any stable system regardless of arrival distribution, service distribution, or number of servers
350	- Generalises to any subsystem: N_queue = X × W
351	
352	### Observation Boundary Effect
353	
354	> [!warning] Exam Trap
355	> In a **short finite trace**, sample mean of inter-arrival gaps **≠ 1/λ**.
356	> Always compute λ = (number of arrivals) / (observation window length).
357	
358	**Worked Example (API Server, 20 s window):**
359	
360	Arrivals at t = 0, 2, 9, 12. Server processes FIFO.
361	
362	| Request | Arrives | Starts | Ends | W | S | R |
363	|---------|---------|--------|------|---|---|---|
364	| A | 0 | 0 | 3 | 0 | 3 | 3 |
365	| B | 2 | 3 | 8 | 1 | 5 | 6 |
366	| C | 9 | 9 | 13 | 0 | 4 | 4 |
367	| D | 12 | 13 | 15 | 1 | 2 | 3 |
368	
369	| Metric | Calculation | Value |
370	|--------|-------------|-------|
371	| λ | 4 / 20 s | **0.2 jobs/s** |
372	| Mean observed gap | (2 + 7 + 3) / 3 | **4 s** |
373	| 1/λ | 1 / 0.2 | **5 s** ← not equal to mean gap |
374	| Mean S | 14 / 4 | **3.5 s** |
375	| U | 14 / 20 | **70%** |
376	
377	Gap mean (4 s) ≠ 1/λ (5 s) because observed gaps only cover t = 0 to t = 12, not the full 20-second window.
378	
379	### M/M/1 Single-Server Queue
380	
381	```mermaid
382	flowchart LR
383	    A["Arrivals\nrate λ\n(Poisson)"] --> Q["🔲🔲🔲\nQueue"]
384	    Q --> SV["⚙️ Server\nrate μ\n(Exponential)"]
385	    SV --> D["Departures\nrate X"]
386	    UT["ρ = λ/μ < 1\nfor stability"]
387	    style UT fill:#ffe0b2,color:#000
388	```
389	
390	- **M** (first) = Markov arrivals (Poisson process)
391	- **M** (second) = Markov service (exponential distribution)
392	- **1** = single server
393	- **Stability:** ρ = λ/μ < 1 (λ < μ)
394	- **Wait in queue:** W = ρ/(1−ρ) × S
395	- **Response time:** R = S / (1−ρ) = W + S

399	## 5. Multi-Server Queues — M/M/c
400	
401	### Structure
402	
403	```mermaid
404	flowchart LR
405	    A["Arrivals\nrate λ"] --> Q["🔲🔲🔲\nSingle Queue"]
406	    Q --> S1["⚙️ Server 1\nrate μ"]
407	    Q --> S2["⚙️ Server 2\nrate μ"]
408	    Q --> S3["⚙️ Server 3\nrate μ"]
409	    S1 --> D["Departures"]
410	    S2 --> D
411	    S3 --> D
412	    label["ρ = λ / (c × μ)"]
413	    style label fill:#ffe0b2,color:#000
414	```
415	
416	### Key Formula
417	
418	$$\rho = \frac{\lambda}{c \times \mu} = \frac{\lambda \times S}{c}$$
419	
420	**Stable if ρ < 1 (i.e. λ < c × μ)**
421	
422	Real-world examples: 3 API servers behind one load balancer, thread pool with c workers, c GPUs sharing one request queue.
423	
424	### One Fast Server vs Many Slow Servers
425	
426	Given the same aggregate capacity (total throughput = c × μ):
427	
428	| Scenario | Latency | Why |
429	|----------|---------|-----|
430	| **1 fast server (rate c×μ)** | **Lower** | Each job gets the full rate c×μ |
431	| **c slow servers (each rate μ)** | Higher | Each job gets only rate μ |
432	
433	**But real systems use many servers because:**
434	- Single device cannot scale up indefinitely
435	- Fault tolerance: one server failing removes only 1/c of capacity
436	
437	> [!tip] The case for many servers is **operational** (fault tolerance, cost, scaling limits), NOT a queueing advantage.
438	
439	### Worked Example — API Tier
440	
441	λ = 8 tps, S = 148 ms, c = 3 servers:
442	
443	| State | ρ per server | Mean wait at API |
444	|-------|-------------|-----------------|
445	| Normal (c = 3) | 8 × 0.148 / 3 = **0.40** | ≈ 7 ms |
446	| One server down (c = 2) | 8 × 0.148 / 2 = **0.60** | ≈ 58 ms (8× worse) |

463	### 6.1 — Forced Flow Law
464	
465	$$X_k = V_k \times X$$
466	
467	All device throughputs are forced into fixed proportion to system throughput by visit counts.

469	> [!example] E.4.1

476	
477	$$D_k = V_k \times S_k$$
478

482	
483	$$U_k = X \times D_k$$
484

487	Also: **D_k = U_k / X** — compute demand from monitoring data without tracing individual visits.

505	## 7. Bottleneck Analysis
506	
507	### Capacity Bottleneck vs Congestion Hotspot
508	
509	```mermaid
510	flowchart TD
511	    A["Rising load:\ncompute ceilings\nfor every device"] --> B["Device with\nlowest ceiling\n= CAPACITY BOTTLENECK"]
512	    B --> C{Is queueing\nactually there?}
513	    C -->|"Yes\n(usual case)"| D["✅ Bottleneck = Hotspot\nFix: reduce demand\nor add capacity"]
514	    C -->|"No\n(variability case)"| E["⚠️ Congestion Hotspot\nis elsewhere\nFix: reduce variance"]
515	    style D fill:#c8e6c9,color:#000
516	    style E fill:#ffccbc,color:#000
517	```
518	
519	| Term | Definition |
520	|------|-----------|
521	| **Capacity Bottleneck** | Device with **lowest throughput ceiling** — first to saturate as load increases |
522	| **Congestion Hotspot** | Device where **queueing actually accumulates** — may differ from bottleneck due to variability |
523	
524	### Throughput Ceilings
525	
526	**Single-server device:**
527	
528	$$X \leq \frac{1}{D_{max}}$$
529	
530	**Device with c servers:**
531	
532	$$X \leq \frac{c}{D}$$
533	
534	> [!warning] The largest demand ≠ the bottleneck when server counts differ!
535	> Always divide by server count to get the ceiling. The bottleneck is the **lowest ceiling**.
536	
537	**Response Time Lower Bound (no queueing anywhere):**
538	
539	$$R \geq D_1 + D_2 + \ldots + D_n$$
540	
541	### Worked Example — Running Case
542	
543	| Device | Servers | Ceiling | |
544	|--------|---------|---------|---|
545	| API tier | 3 | 3 / 0.148 = **20.3 tps** | Not the bottleneck |
546	| Database | 1 | 1 / 0.078 = **12.8 tps** | ← **Lowest = bottleneck** |
547	| Storage | 2 | 2 / 0.016 = **125 tps** | Far from binding |
548	
549	Minimum response time: R ≥ 148 + 78 + 16 = **242 ms**
550	
551	A target of 20 tps is infeasible without changing the database.
552	
553	### Worked Example — Wafer Fab (E.4.3 / E.4.4)
554	
555	| Step | D | Ceiling (1 tool) |
556	|------|---|-----------------|
557	| Deposition | 6.7 h | 3.6 lots/day |
558	| **Photolithography** | **8.6 h** | **2.8 lots/day** ← bottleneck |
559	| Etch | 5.4 h | 4.4 lots/day |
560	| Ion implant | 3.2 h | 7.5 lots/day |
561	| CMP | 2.6 h | 9.2 lots/day |
562	| Metrology | 1.6 h | 15 lots/day |
563	
564	**E.4.3 answer:** Bottleneck = photolithography; X ≤ 2.8 lots/day.
565	
566	**E.4.4 (c = 3 litho tools):** Litho ceiling = 3/8.6 = 8.4 lots/day → deposition (3.6 lots/day) becomes new binding ceiling.
567	
568	**One tool fails (c = 2):** Litho ceiling = 2/8.6 = 5.6 lots/day. With λ = 3.05 lots/day, **still no saturation** — rising queue is a variability effect, not a capacity shortfall.
569	
570	### Three Levers to Fix a Bottleneck
571	
572	Since D = V × S:
573	
574	| Lever | How | Example |
575	|-------|-----|---------|
576	| **Reduce V** | Cache results → fewer visits to device | DB visits: 4 → 2 (halves D) |
577	| **Reduce S** | Index, optimise query | Each visit faster |
578	| **Add capacity** | Replicas, faster hardware | Ceiling rises |
579	
580	> [!tip] Optimisation is iterative — fix one bottleneck, recompute ceilings, find the next one.

607	| **Open** | Unbounded external population | None | Web server, API gateway |
608	| **Closed** | Fixed N users cycling | Z (average think time) | Load testing tools, DB connection pools |
609	
610	### Interactive Response Time Law
611	
612	Apply Little's Law to the whole system including users:
613	
614	$$N = X \times (R + Z)$$
615	
616	Rearranging:
617	
618	$$\boxed{R = \frac{N}{X} - Z}$$
619	
620	**Interpretation:**
621	- Tool fixes N (virtual users) and Z (think time)
622	- Tool measures X (throughput)
623	- Law gives R (experienced response time)
624	
625	> [!example] E.4.5
626	> N = 200 users, Z = 10 s, X = 18 tps
627	> R = 200/18 − 10 = 11.11 − 10 = **1.11 seconds**
628	
629	> [!warning] Doubling users when throughput is capped at the bottleneck ceiling → all extra N appears as extra R, not extra X.
630	
631	---
632	
633	## 9. Variability and the Kingman Formula
634	
635	### Coefficient of Variation
636	
637	$$C = \frac{\text{standard deviation}}{\text{mean}}$$
638	
639	| Symbol | Measures | Value = 0 | Value = 1 | Value > 1 |
640	|--------|----------|-----------|-----------|-----------|
641	| **Cₐ** | Inter-arrival time variability | Perfectly regular arrivals | Poisson (M/M/1 assumption) | Bursty arrivals |
642	| **Cₛ** | Service time variability | Fixed service time | Exponential (M/M/1 assumption) | Mixed workload |
643	
644	> [!example] High Cₛ trap
645	> An API serving mostly 20 ms lookups plus occasional 5-second report queries has very high Cₛ, even though the **mean** service time looks moderate. Averages hide this completely.
646	
647	### The Kingman Formula (G/G/1 — single server)
648	
649	$$\boxed{W \approx \underbrace{\frac{\rho}{1-\rho}}_{\text{utilisation}} \times \underbrace{\frac{C_a^2 + C_s^2}{2}}_{\text{variability}} \times \underbrace{S}_{\text{service time}}}$$
650	
651	```mermaid
652	flowchart LR
653	    U["Utilisation term\nρ/(1−ρ)\nSteep growth near ρ=1\nSame as M/M/1 shape"]
654	    V["Variability term\n(Ca²+Cs²)/2\nScales curve up/down\n= 1 when Ca=Cs=1 → M/M/1"]
655	    S["Service time S\nAnchor for time scale"]
656	    U & V & S --> W["W ≈ U × V × S"]
657	    style W fill:#ffd700,color:#000
658	```
659	
660	- At Ca = Cs = 1: reduces exactly to the **M/M/1 result**
661	- Formula is **approximate** for G/G/1, but excellent for first-order reasoning
662	
663	### Worked Comparison (E.4.6 style)
664	
665	All three scenarios: **ρ = 0.8, S = 100 ms**. Utilisation term = 0.8/0.2 = **4**.
666	
667	| Scenario | Ca² | Cs² | Variability term | **W** |
668	|----------|-----|-----|----------------|-------|
669	| Regular (deterministic) | 0 | 0 | 0 | **≈ 0 ms** |
670	| Markov (M/M/1) | 1 | 1 | 1 | 4 × 1 × 100 = **400 ms** |
671	| Mixed workload | 1 | 4 | 2.5 | 4 × 2.5 × 100 = **1,000 ms** |
672	
673	Same hardware, same load, same mean service time → **2.5× more waiting** from variance alone.
674	
675	> [!example] E.4.6
676	> ρ = 0.9, S = 50 ms. Utilisation term = 9.
677	> - Ca² = Cs² = 1: W ≈ 9 × 1 × 50 = **450 ms**
678	> - Ca² = 1, Cs² = 9: W ≈ 9 × 5 × 50 = **2,250 ms**
679	>
680	> Five times longer wait purely from service time variance.
681	
682	### Sakasegawa's G/G/c Approximation (Multi-Server)
683	
684	$$W \approx \frac{C_a^2 + C_s^2}{2} \times \frac{\rho^{\sqrt{2(c+1)}-1}}{c(1-\rho)} \times S$$
685	
686	Same three-factor structure as Kingman with a modified utilisation term for c servers.
687	
688	Use to **understand the mechanism** (what grew, and why) rather than as a precise point predictor.
689	
690	### Variability in Practice
691	
692	| Situation | Mechanism | Fix |
693	|-----------|-----------|-----|
694	| **Mixed workloads** (long + short requests) | High Cₛ | Split into separate queues (reduces Cₛ) |
695	| **Bursty arrivals** (retry storms, scheduled jobs) | High Cₐ | Jittered retries, request smoothing |
696	| **Headroom rule** | Both | Run interactive systems below 70–80% U |
697	| **LLM inference** | Token count varies → high Cₛ | Continuous batching; separate prefill from decode |
698	
699	### Running Case Diagnosis
700	
701	Database service time distribution shows **two populations**:
702	
703	```
704	Frequency
705	   ↑
706	   │  ████  ←── Standard queries ~5 ms (many)
707	   │  ████
708	   │  ████
709	   │  █░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░█  ←── Report queries ~375 ms (few)
710	   └──────────────────────────────────────→ Service time
711	      5ms                            375ms
712	```
713	
714	Cs² ≈ **34** at the database — extreme. One report query ≈ 75 standard queries of work. Mean = 19.4 ms. Almost no query actually takes 19.4 ms.
715	
716	**Fix:** Move report queries to a read replica (DB-RPT).
717	
718	| Metric | BEFORE | AFTER |
719	|--------|--------|-------|
720	| DB-01 Cs² | ≈ 34 | ≈ 0 |
721	| DB-01 wait per query | 165 ms | 5 ms |
722	| Transaction p95 | 3.48 s | **0.44 s** (8× improvement) |
723	
724	**Kingman Validation on DB-RPT:**
725	
726	```
727	Inputs: ρ = 0.23, Ca² = 1.0, Cs² = 0.26, S = 1.43 s
728	Predicted W ≈ (0.23/0.77) × (1.26/2) × 1.43 ≈ 0.30 s
729	Measured W = 0.27 s  (within 8%) ✓
730	```
731	
732	> [!warning] Kingman caveat
733	> The same check on shared DB-01 (BEFORE) over-predicts by 2–3×. In a network, arrivals feed back on themselves — they are not independent. **Kingman is precise where its assumptions hold; a mechanism-teacher everywhere else.**
734	
735	---
736	
737	## 10. Four Sources Framework
738	
739	Every performance problem traces to one of four root causes. Diagnose which is binding **before** touching anything.
740	
741	```mermaid
742	mindmap
743	  root((Performance\nProblem))
744	    DEMAND
745	      D = V × S
746	      High D → high U
747	      Lever: reduce V or S
748	    CAPACITY
749	      X ≤ c / Dmax
750	      Throughput plateaus
751	      Lever: add servers or replicas
752	    VARIABILITY
753	      Kingman / Sakasegawa
754	      High R despite moderate U
755	      Lever: separate queues, jitter
756	    POPULATION
757	      R = N/X − Z
758	      R grows with user count
759	      Lever: reduce N or increase X
760	```
761	
762	| Source | Formula | Key symptom | Fix |
763	|--------|---------|-------------|-----|
764	| **Demand** | D = V × S | High U, bottleneck shifts unexpectedly | Reduce V (cache) or S (index) |
765	| **Capacity** | X ≤ c/D | Throughput plateaus; adding load has no effect | Add servers, replicas, faster hardware |
766	| **Variability** | Kingman / Sakasegawa | High tail latency at moderate U; individual requests vary wildly | Separate heavy/light; jitter arrivals |
767	| **Population** | R = N/X − Z | R grows with user count even when X is unconstrained | Reduce N or increase throughput ceiling |
768	
769	### Applying the Diagnosis
770	
771	| Case | Demand | Capacity | Variability | Population | Root cause |
772	|------|--------|----------|-------------|------------|------------|
773	| Online service BEFORE | Unchanged | Not binding (X = 8.06 vs ceiling 12.8) | **Cs² ≈ 34** at DB | Open system | **Variability** |
774	| Wafer fab (LITHO-02 down) | Unchanged | Reduced but not binding (λ = 3.05 vs ceiling 5.6) | **Cₐ ≈ 1.5** amplified | Open system | **Variability** |
775	
776	---
777	
778	## 11. All Worked Examples — Assignments
779	
780	### E.4.1 — Forced Flow Law
781	
782	> Each web transaction issues 4 SQL queries. Web server completes 25 tps. What must the database sustain?
783	
784	X(db) = V × X = 4 × 25 = **100 queries/second**
785	
786	---
787	
788	### E.4.2 — Service Demand Law
789	
790	> From E.4.1: each query takes 5 ms. What is DB demand per transaction, and DB utilisation at 30 tps?
791	
792	D(db) = V × S = 4 × 5 = **20 ms per transaction**
793	U(db) = X × D = 30 × 0.020 = **0.60 (60%)**
794	
795	---
796	
797	### E.4.3 — Bottleneck Analysis (single server per step)
798	
799	> Fab demands: deposition 6.7 h, litho 8.6 h, etch 5.4 h, ion implant 3.2 h, CMP 2.6 h, metrology 1.6 h. All single tools. Bottleneck?
800	
801	Largest demand = litho at 8.6 h.
802	X ≤ 1/8.6 lots/h = 24/8.6 ≈ **2.8 lots/day**
803	
804	---
805	
806	### E.4.4 — Bottleneck Analysis (multi-server)
807	
808	> Three litho tools behind one queue. New ceiling? One tool fails — does the fab saturate at λ = 3.05 lots/day?
809	
810	With c = 3: litho ceiling = 3/8.6 ≈ 8.4 lots/day.
811	New binding ceiling = deposition = 24/6.7 ≈ **3.6 lots/day**
812	
813	One tool fails (c = 2): litho ceiling = 2/8.6 ≈ **5.6 lots/day** > 3.6 > 3.05 → **fab does not saturate**. Rising queue = variability effect.
814	
815	---
816	
817	### E.4.5 — Interactive Response Time Law
818	
819	> N = 200 users, Z = 10 s, X = 18 tps. What is R?
820	
821	R = N/X − Z = 200/18 − 10 = 11.11 − 10 = **1.11 seconds**
822	
823	---
824	
825	### E.4.6 — Kingman Formula
826	
827	> ρ = 0.9, S = 50 ms. Estimate W when (i) Ca² = Cs² = 1, (ii) Ca² = 1, Cs² = 9.
828	
829	Utilisation term = ρ/(1−ρ) = 0.9/0.1 = 9.
830	
831	(i) W ≈ 9 × (1+1)/2 × 50 = 9 × 1 × 50 = **450 ms**
832	(ii) W ≈ 9 × (1+9)/2 × 50 = 9 × 5 × 50 = **2,250 ms**
833	
834	5× increase purely from variance.
835	
836	---
837	
838	### Workload Exercises
839	
840	**Manufacturing:**
841	
842	| Question | Working | Answer |
843	|----------|---------|--------|
844	| Average rate | 120,000 / (20 × 8 hr) | 750 units/hr |
845	| U at average rate | 750 × 4/3600 | **83%** |
846	| Final-week rate | 48,000 / (5 × 8 hr) | 1,200 units/hr |
847	| U at final-week rate | 1,200 × 4/3600 = 1.33 | **133% — overloaded** |
848	
849	**Healthcare (polyclinic):**
850	
851	| Question | Working | Answer |
852	|----------|---------|--------|
853	| Total arrivals | 60 × 70% + 25 | 67 patients/hr |
854	| U at 67/hr | μ = 80/hr; 67/80 | **83.8%** — coping |
855	| With flu drive | 82/80 | **102.5% — overloaded** |
856	
857	**IT Flash Sale:**
858	
859	| Question | Working | Answer |
860	|----------|---------|--------|
861	| Arrivals in first minute | 500,000 × 4% / 60 s | 333 arrivals/s |
862	| Product service req/s | 333 × 6 | 2,000 req/s |
863	| Servers at 70% U | ⌈2,000 / 70⌉ | **29 servers** |
864	| Peak:average ratio | 2,000 / 40 | **50×** |
865	
866	---
867	
868	## 12. Case Study Summaries
869	
870	### Online Service — Three Windows
871	
872	```mermaid
873	flowchart LR
874	    B["BEFORE\n8 days\nc=3 API servers\nρ(db)=0.63\nCs²≈34\np95 = 3.48 s\n⚠️ Problem hidden\nin averages"] -->|"API-02 fails"| DEG
875	    DEG["DEGRADED\nc=2 API servers\nAPI wait 7→58 ms\nDB still bottleneck\nMade worse but\nnot the cause"] -->|"API-02 restored\n+ DB split"| AFT
876	    AFT["AFTER\nc=3 API servers\nDB-01 Cs²≈0\nDB-RPT separate\np95 = 0.44 s\n✅ 8× improvement"]
877	```
878	
879	**Root cause:** Cs² ≈ 34 at the database from mixed workload (standard + report queries).
880	**Fix:** Separate queues by traffic type → attack the variance, not the load.
881	
882	### Wafer Fab — LITHO-02 Failure
883	
884	| Metric | January (Healthy) | June (Problem) |
885	|--------|------------------|---------------|
886	| Tools in litho | 3 | 2 (LITHO-02 degraded) |
887	| ρ per tool | 0.36 | 0.54 |
888	| Litho queue time | Baseline | **3× higher** |
889	| Cycle time | 1.8 days | **2.2 days** |
890	| Throughput | Still 3.05 lots/day | Still 3.05 lots/day |
891	
892	**Why not a capacity problem:** With λ = 3.05 and ceiling = 5.6 (c=2), the fab **never saturates**.
893	**Why a variability problem:** High Cₐ ≈ 1.5 (bursty arrivals) combined with higher ρ inflated wait via Sakasegawa's formula.
894	
895	Priority discipline: Hot lots — 3.2 h queue; Normal lots — 8.0 h queue.
896	
897	---
898	
899	## 13. Formula Quick Reference
900	
901	| Formula | Name | Notes |
902	|---------|------|-------|
903	| R = W + S | Response time | Always |
904	| U = X × S | Utilisation Law | General; use U = λS only when stable |
905	| N = X × R | Little's Law | Any stable system |
906	| ρ = λ/(c × μ) | M/M/c traffic intensity | c = 1 gives M/M/1 |
907	| X_k = V_k × X | Forced Flow Law | Device throughput from system throughput |
908	| D_k = V_k × S_k | Service demand | Total service time per transaction at device k |
909	| U_k = X × D_k | Service Demand Law | Utilisation Law per device using demands |
910	| X ≤ 1/D_max | Throughput ceiling (1 server) | |
911	| X ≤ c/D | Throughput ceiling (c servers) | Lowest ceiling = bottleneck |
912	| R ≥ Σ D_k | Response time lower bound | Best possible R when no queueing |
913	| R = N/X − Z | Interactive Response Time Law | Closed systems; derived from N = X(R+Z) |
914	| C = σ/mean | Coefficient of variation | Cₐ for arrivals, Cₛ for service |
915	| W ≈ [ρ/(1−ρ)] × [(Ca²+Cs²)/2] × S | Kingman (G/G/1) | Ca=Cs=1 reduces to M/M/1 |
916	| W ≈ [(Ca²+Cs²)/2] × [ρ^(√(2(c+1))−1) / c(1−ρ)] × S | Sakasegawa (G/G/c) | Multi-server Kingman |
917	
918	### Utilisation Law — Calculator
919	
920	| Given | Find | Calculation |
921	|-------|------|-------------|
922	| λ = 3/s, S = 100 ms | U | 3 × 0.1 = **30%** |
923	| U = 0.9, λ = 100/s | S | 0.9/100 = **9 ms** |
924	| S = 10 ms | λ_max (at U=1) | 1/0.01 = **100 tps** |
925	| λ = 8 tps, S = 0.148 s, c = 3 | ρ | 8 × 0.148/3 = **0.395** |
926	
927	### Kingman — Calculator
928	
929	| ρ | 1−ρ | ρ/(1−ρ) |
930	|---|-----|---------|
931	| 0.5 | 0.5 | 1.0 |
932	| 0.6 | 0.4 | 1.5 |
933	| 0.7 | 0.3 | 2.33 |
934	| 0.8 | 0.2 | 4.0 |
935	| 0.9 | 0.1 | 9.0 |
936	| 0.95 | 0.05 | 19.0 |
937	
938	---
939	
940	## Exam Strategy Checklist
941	
942	> [!tip] For any performance question:
943	> 1. **Identify which of the Four Sources is at play** (Demand / Capacity / Variability / Population)
944	> 2. **Draw the system** — identify devices, visit counts V, server counts c
945	> 3. **Compute demands** D_k = V_k × S_k
946	> 4. **Compute ceilings** c/D for each device → find bottleneck (lowest ceiling)
947	> 5. **Apply the right formula** based on what is asked (Kingman = variability; Interactive Law = closed system; Forced Flow = device throughput)
948	> 6. **Check if the answer makes sense** — U should be < 1 in a stable system; R should be ≥ S
949	
950	> [!warning] Common Exam Mistakes
951	> - Using λ instead of X in Utilisation Law when the system is overloaded
952	> - Confusing **capacity bottleneck** (lowest ceiling) with **largest demand** (not the same when c differs)
953	> - Forgetting to divide demand by server count c when computing the ceiling
954	> - Computing 1/λ from the mean of observed inter-arrival gaps instead of from the full window
955	> - Assuming the largest-demand device is automatically the congestion hotspot — it may not be if variability is driving the queue elsewhere

33	
34	## §1 — Foundations
35	
36	### The CIA Triad
37	
38	> [!warning] Most Examined Concept
39	> Every security control maps back to one or more CIA properties. Always state *which* property a technique supports in exam answers.
40	
41	| Property | Meaning | Supported by |
42	|----------|---------|--------------|
43	| **Confidentiality** | Only authorised parties can read the data | Symmetric encryption, asymmetric encryption |
44	| **Integrity** | Data has not been altered in transit or at rest | Hashing, digital signatures |
45	| **Availability** | Systems and data are accessible when needed | Backups, redundancy, DoS defences |
46	
47	### The Threat Model (Alice, Bob, Eve)
48	
49	```
50	Alice ──[plaintext]──► Encrypt(key) ──[ciphertext]──► Decrypt(key) ──[plaintext]──► Bob
51	                                              │
52	                                              ▼
53	                                          Eve (eavesdropper)
54	                                    sees ciphertext; cannot read it
55	                                    without the key
56	```
57	
58	Eve can **intercept** the ciphertext on the insecure channel, but without the key the data is unintelligible.
59	
60	### Types of Cryptography
61	
62	| Type | Keys | Direction | CIA Goal |
63	|------|------|-----------|----------|
64	| **Symmetric** | Single shared key | Enc + Dec with the same key | Confidentiality |
65	| **Asymmetric** | Key pair (public + private) | Public enc / private dec (or reversed) | Confidentiality **or** Authentication |
66	| **Hashing** | No keys | One-way only (no decryption) | Integrity, Authentication (signatures) |
67	
68	---
69	
70	## §2 — Symmetric Cryptography
71	
72	### Classical Ciphers
73	
74	#### Substitution Ciphers — *change the characters*
75	
76	| Cipher | Mechanism | Example |
77	|--------|-----------|---------|
78	| **Caesar** (monoalphabetic) | Shift every letter by a fixed amount | Shift 3: `HELLO` → `KHOOR` |
79	| **Vigenère** (polyalphabetic) | Repeating keyword drives a different shift per position | Key `ALICE`, `HELLO` → `HPTNS` |
80	
81	> [!note] Mono vs Poly
82	> Monoalphabetic = one fixed substitution alphabet → vulnerable to frequency analysis.
83	> Polyalphabetic = multiple alphabets keyed to position → resists simple frequency analysis.
84	
85	#### Transposition Ciphers — *move the characters*
86	
87	| Cipher | Mechanism | Example |
88	|--------|-----------|---------|
89	| **Simple reversal** | Reverse the string | `UNIVERSITY` → `YTISREVINU` |
90	| **Rail Fence** | Write in zig-zag across N rails, read row by row | `HELLOBOB` / 2 rails → `HLOOELBB` |
91	| **Columnar Transposition** | Write into grid row-by-row; read columns in keyword order | Key `RED`, `HELLOWORLD` → `LWLX EORX HLOD` |
92	
93	### Kerckhoffs's Principle
94	
95	> *"The security of a cryptosystem must not depend on the secrecy of the algorithm; it should only depend on the secrecy of the **key**."*
96	
97	**Implication:** even if an attacker knows exactly how Caesar cipher works, they still can't decrypt without the shift key. Design systems so that the *algorithm* can be public — only the *key* must remain secret.
98	
99	### Modern Symmetric Algorithms
100	
101	| Algorithm | Key Length | Block Size | Status |
102	|-----------|-----------|------------|--------|
103	| **DES** | 56-bit effective | 64-bit | **Broken** — cracked in <24 hrs (2002); 16 rounds of S-P-XOR |
104	| **3DES** | 168-bit (3×56) | 64-bit | **Deprecated from 2024** — small block vulnerable to birthday attacks; uses Ek1 → Dk2 → Ek3 |
105	| **AES** | 128 / 192 / 256-bit | 128-bit | **Current standard** — theoretically vulnerable to quantum computing |
106	
107	> [!tip] DES → 3DES → AES progression
108	> Increasing key length is driven by increasing computing power making shorter keys brute-forceable.
109	
110	### One-Time Pad (OTP)
111	
112	- Key is **at least as long as the plaintext**; used **once only**; must be **truly random**
113	- **Theoretically unbreakable** — but impractical at scale (key distribution problem)
114	- Real-world analogues: 2FA codes, hardware dongles
115	
116	### Random Number Generators
117	
118	| Type | Source | Security |
119	|------|--------|----------|
120	| **True RNG** | Physical entropy: mouse movement, fan noise, thermal noise | Cryptographically strong |
121	| **Pseudo RNG** | Mathematical formula + seed | **Predictable if seed is known** — do not use for OTP keys |
122
