124	
125	## §3 — Asymmetric Cryptography
126	
127	### The Key Distribution Problem
128	
129	Symmetric crypto requires the shared key to reach the recipient securely *before* communication begins — but on an insecure channel, how? Asymmetric crypto solves this.
130	
131	### Key Pair Roles
132	
133	```
134	Default roles:
135	  Public key  ──► ENCRYPTS  (anyone can send you a confidential message)
136	  Private key ──► DECRYPTS  (only you can read it)
137	
138	Reversed roles:
139	  Private key ──► ENCRYPTS  (proves the message came from you — "signing")
140	  Public key  ──► DECRYPTS  (anyone can verify the signature)
141	```
142	
143	### Confidentiality vs Authentication
144	
145	| Goal | Encrypt with | Decrypt with |
146	|------|-------------|-------------|
147	| **Confidentiality** | Recipient's **public** key | Recipient's **private** key |
148	| **Authentication** | Sender's **private** key | Sender's **public** key |
149	
150	#### Combined (Authentication + Confidentiality)
151	
152	Alice sends a secure, authenticated message to Bob:
153	
154	1. Alice encrypts with **her own private key** → signs it
155	2. Alice encrypts result with **Bob's public key** → sealed for Bob only
156	3. Bob decrypts with **his private key** → unseals
157	4. Bob decrypts again with **Alice's public key** → verifies Alice's signature
158	
159	### One-Way Functions
160	
161	The security of asymmetric crypto relies on problems easy to compute forward but infeasible to reverse:
162	
163	| Problem | Easy direction | Hard direction |
164	|---------|---------------|----------------|
165	| **Modular arithmetic** | Compute `a mod n` | Recover `a` from result alone |
166	| **Prime factorisation** | Multiply two primes: `p × q = n` | Factor `n` back to `p` and `q` |
167	| **Discrete logarithm** | Compute `G^a mod p` | Recover `a` from `G^a mod p` |
168	
169	### RSA
170	
171	**Key generation (know all 6 steps):**
172	
173	1. Pick two large distinct primes `p` and `q`
174	2. Compute `n = p × q`
175	3. Compute Euler's totient: `φ(n) = (p−1)(q−1)`
176	4. Pick `e` where `1 < e < φ(n)` and `gcd(e, φ(n)) = 1`
177	5. Compute `d` such that `d × e ≡ 1 mod φ(n)`
178	6. **Public key = (e, n)** · **Private key = (d, n)**
179	
180	> [!warning] Common RSA Confusion
181	> Encryption/decryption use modulus `n`. Key *generation* uses modulus `φ(n)`. These are different.
182	
183	**Security foundation:** knowing `e` and `n` (both public) does not let you compute `d` without factoring `n`.
184	
185	### Diffie–Hellman Key Exchange
186	
187	> [!important]
188	> DH is **not** encryption — it establishes a **shared secret key** that both parties can then use with a symmetric cipher. No key is ever transmitted.
189	
190	**Setup:** publicly agree on prime `p` and generator `G`.
191	
192	```
193	Alice                             Bob
194	Choose secret a                   Choose secret b
195	A = G^a mod p ────────────────►
196	              ◄──────────────── B = G^b mod p
197	K = B^a mod p                     K = A^b mod p
198	Both arrive at K = G^(ab) mod p   (same shared secret)
199	```
200	
201	An eavesdropper sees `p`, `G`, `A`, `B` — but cannot compute `K` without solving the discrete logarithm problem.
202	
203	---
204	
205	## §4 — Hashing, Digital Signatures & Cryptanalysis
206	
207	### Hash Functions
208	
209	A hash function takes **arbitrary-length input** → produces **fixed-length digest**. It is **one-way**: given the digest, you cannot recover the input.
210	
211	**Two required properties:**
212	1. **One-way (pre-image resistance)** — cannot find a message `m` such that `hash(m) = h`
213	2. **Strong collision resistance** — cannot find two *different* messages `m₁ ≠ m₂` where `hash(m₁) = hash(m₂)`
214	
215	**CIA contribution:** primarily **Integrity**; combined with signing → Authentication.
216	
217	| Algorithm | Digest Size | Status |
218	|-----------|------------|--------|
219	| **MD5** | 128 bits | **Broken** — collision demonstrated 2004 |
220	| **SHA-1** | 160 bits | **Broken** — practical collision demonstrated |
221	| **SHA-256** | 256 bits | Currently secure |
222	| **SHA-384 / SHA-512** | 384 / 512 bits | Currently secure |
223	
224	### Digital Signatures
225	
226	```mermaid
227	flowchart LR
228	    Doc["Document"] --> H["Hash(doc)"]
229	    H --> Enc["Encrypt with\nSender's PRIVATE key"]
230	    Enc --> Sig["Digital Signature"]
231	    Sig --> Send["Send: Doc + Sig"]
232	
233	    Send --> RecHash["Hash received doc"]
234	    Send --> DecSig["Decrypt Sig with\nSender's PUBLIC key"]
235	    RecHash --> Cmp{"Compare\nhashes"}
236	    DecSig --> Cmp
237	    Cmp --> |"Match"| OK["✅ Authentic + Intact"]
238	    Cmp --> |"Mismatch"| FAIL["❌ Tampered or Wrong Sender"]
239	```
240	
241	**Provides:** Authenticity (who sent it) + Integrity (not altered). Not confidentiality on its own (document is still visible unless separately encrypted).
242	
243	### Birthday Attack
244	
245	Named after the birthday paradox: in a group of 23 people, >50% chance two share a birthday — because you're comparing *every pair*, not one against all.
246	
247	**Applied to hashing:** finding *any two inputs* that produce the same hash is far easier than finding a second input matching a *specific* hash. This is why 64-bit blocks (DES) and 128-bit digests (MD5) are insecure — the effective collision resistance is only half the digest length in bits.
248	
249	### Cryptanalysis — Attacking Ciphers
250	
251	| Attack | What the attacker has | What they do | Best against |
252	|--------|----------------------|--------------|--------------|
253	| **Brute Force** | Just ciphertext | Try every possible key; needs ~half the keyspace on average | Small key spaces / weak algorithms |
254	| **Frequency Analysis** | Just ciphertext | Count letter frequencies; E=12.51%, T, A, O, I most common | Monoalphabetic substitution and transposition ciphers |
255	| **Known Plaintext** | Both plaintext + its ciphertext | Infer key from `C = (P + K) mod 26` | Any cipher where paired samples are obtainable |
256	
257	> [!note] Frequency Analysis — Key Fact
258	> Transposition ciphers change character *positions* but not their *frequencies* — so frequency analysis still works on them.
259	
260	---
261	
262	## §5 — Steganography
263	
264	### Steganography vs. Cryptography
265	
266	| | Cryptography | Steganography |
267	|---|---|---|
268	| **Hides** | Content of the message | **Existence** of the message |
269	| **What the attacker sees** | Obviously encrypted data | An ordinary-looking file |
270	| **CIA contribution** | Confidentiality | Obscurity (security through obscurity) |
271	
272	> The two can be **combined**: encrypt the payload first, then hide the ciphertext in a cover object.
273	
274	### The Core Process
275	
276	```
277	Payload  ───┐
278	            ├──► Steganography algorithm ──► Stego Object (looks like an ordinary file)
279	Cover Object ──┘
280	```
281	
282	- **Payload** — the secret data to hide
283	- **Cover Object** — the carrier (image, audio, text)
284	- **Stego Object** — the output that contains the hidden payload
285	
286	Steganography exploits **redundancy**: parts of the carrier file that can be altered without perceptible change.
287	
288	### LSB (Least Significant Bit) Algorithms
289	
290	Each RGB pixel byte has 8 bits. Changing **only the rightmost bit** causes a ≤1/255 change to the pixel value — visually imperceptible.
291	
292	> [!warning] Format Constraint
293	> LSB works **only on lossless formats** (PNG, TIFF, BMP). Lossy compression (JPEG) destroys embedded LSB data.
294	
295	| Variant | How it works | Statistical detectability |
296	|---------|-------------|--------------------------|
297	| **LSB Replacement** | Directly replace LSB of cover pixel with payload bit | Higher — creates detectable asymmetry |
298	| **LSB Matching** | If LSB ≠ payload bit, randomly ±1 the pixel value | Lower — avoids hard-flip pattern |
299	
300	**Capacity:** only **50% of LSBs change on average** (Replacement), since half already match the payload bit.
301	
302	### Bit Planes
303	
304	Each colour channel decomposes into **8 bit planes** (one per bit position, 0 = LSB, 7 = MSB):
305	
306	- **High planes** (7, 6, 5) → retain the visible structure of the image
307	- **Low planes** (0, 1, 2) → look like random noise
308	
309	This explains why LSB changes are invisible: the 0th plane already appears as noise.
310	
311	### BPCS (Bit Plane Complexity Segmentation)
312	
313	Instead of always using the LSB plane, hide data in **any complex (noisy) region** of any bit plane.
314	
315	**Complexity measure** for an 8-byte segment/block:
316	
317	```
318	c = (number of bit-value transitions) / 112
319	
320	where 112 = 2 × 8 rows × 7 max transitions per row
321	
322	If c > T (threshold, typically 0.3) → segment is "complex" → usable for hiding
323	```
324	
325	**Algorithm:**
326	```
327	While payload remains:
328	    Get next bit plane
329	    For each complex segment in the plane:
330	        Get next payload block
331	        If payload block is complex: hide it directly
332	        Else: conjugate (XOR) it to make it complex, then hide it
333	```
334	
335	**Advantage over LSB:** can hide more data without visible degradation; uses any bit plane, not just the least significant.
336	
337	### Steganalysis (Attacking Steganography)
338	
339	| Technique | Method |
340	|-----------|--------|
341	| **Visual** | Black-and-white filter (even pixels → black, odd → white) makes LSB changes visible; difference image between original and stego |
342	| **Statistical** | Analyse pixel-value distribution for irregularities introduced by embedding |
343	| **Tool-based** | Automated detection software |
344	
345	---
346	
347	## §6 — Access Control
348	
349	### The Three-Stage Pipeline
350	
351	```
352	Identification ──► Authentication ──► Authorisation
353	 (who are you?)   (prove it)          (what can you do?)
354	```
355	
356	### Authentication Categories (The Three Factors)
357	
358	> [!tip] Exam Mnemonic
359	> **KTB** — **K**nowledge / **T**oken / **B**iometrics
360	
361	| Factor | Basis | Examples |
362	|--------|-------|----------|
363	| **Knowledge** | Something you **know** | Password, passphrase, PIN, graphical password |
364	| **Token** | Something you **have** | Smart card, eToken, RFID tag, mobile device |
365	| **Biometrics** | Something you **are** | Fingerprint, iris, retina, face, gait, voice |
366	
367	**Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA/2FA):** combines two or more factor types — significantly stronger than any single factor.
368	
369	### Passwords
370	
371	#### Secure Storage — Progressive Hardening
372	
373	| Method | Weakness |
374	|--------|----------|
375	| Store **plaintext** | One breach = all passwords exposed |
376	| Store **encrypted** | Reversible — key compromise = all exposed |
377	| Store **Hash(password)** | Vulnerable to precomputed rainbow tables |
378	| Store **Hash(password + salt)** ✅ | **Best** — salt defeats precomputed tables |
379	
380	**Salt:** a random string appended before hashing. Since each user gets a unique salt, attackers cannot reuse precomputed tables — every password must be cracked individually.
381	
382	#### Password Attacks
383	
384	| Attack | Method | Defence |
385	|--------|--------|---------|
386	| **Brute Force** | Try all combinations | Long passwords; account lockout |
387	| **Dictionary Attack** | Try known/common passwords + variants | Avoid dictionary words; salted hashing |
388	| **Rainbow Table** | Precomputed hash→password lookup | **Salting** renders these useless |
389	| **Social Engineering** | Mine personal details from social media | User education; avoid personal passwords |
390	| **Google Dorking** | `ext:csv inurl:passwd` — find exposed credential files | Correct file permissions; proper .htaccess |
391	
392	#### Passphrase Technique
393	`"i love to watch physical 100 on netflix every friday, saturday and sunday"` → take nth letter of each word → `iltwp100one56a7` (long, memorable, not in any dictionary)
394	
395	### Graphical Authentication
396	
397	| Type | Method | Vulnerability |
398	|------|--------|--------------|
399	| **Recognition-based** | Pick passimages from challenge set | Shoulder surfing |
400	| **Cued-recall** | Click specific points on an image | "Hotspots" — people click obvious features |
401	| **Recall-based** | Draw a pattern (e.g. Android unlock) | Smudge attacks; limited effective pattern space |
402	
403	Password space for recognition-based: `(set_size)^(rounds)` — e.g. 1 of 9 images, 5 rounds → 9⁵ = 59,049.
404	
405	### Token Authentication
406	
407	| Token | Technology | Key Features |
408	|-------|-----------|--------------|
409	| **eToken** | USB key / smart card / mobile | Stores keys/certificates; 2FA; digital signing |
410	| **Smart Card** | Embedded microprocessor | JavaCard/MULTOS multi-app; PIN storage; tamper-resistant |
411	| **RFID Tag** | RF-powered IC + antenna | Passive (reader-powered) or active (battery); ~2KB storage |
412	
413	**RFID vulnerabilities:** OTA spoof, MITM sniffing, side-channel power analysis.
414	
415	### Biometric Authentication
416	
417	#### Requirements of a Good Biometric
418	
419	> [!note] Acronym: UDPC
420	> **U**niversality · **D**istinctiveness · **P**ermanence · **C**ollectability
421	
422	| Property | Meaning |
423	|----------|---------|
424	| **Universality** | Every person must have the characteristic |
425	| **Distinctiveness** | Any two people differ sufficiently |
426	| **Permanence** | Characteristic stays stable over time |
427	| **Collectability** | Can be quantitatively measured |
428	
429	#### Accuracy Metrics
430	
431	- **FAR (False Accept Rate)** — wrongly grants access to an impostor (ideally 0)
432	- **TAR (True Accept Rate)** — correctly grants access to the legitimate user (ideally 1)
433	- **ROC curve** — plots TAR vs FAR across threshold settings; higher TAR typically means higher FAR
434	
435	#### Biometric Modality Comparison
436	
437	| Modality | Uniqueness | Accuracy | Speed | Cost | Notes |
438	|----------|-----------|----------|-------|------|-------|
439	| **Retinal** | ~400 features | Most accurate (~20 000× fingerprint) | 15 s enrol; ≥10 s verify | $100K+ | Most invasive; changes with glaucoma |
440	| **Iris** | 256 features | FAR ~1 in 10M; more than fingerprint | Few seconds enrol; <5 s verify | $200–$2000 | Less invasive than retinal; equal in twins |
441	| **Fingerprint** | ~1 in 64B | ~1 in 100K false positive | <1 s (contactless); 5–10 s (contact) | $30–$1000 | Affected by dryness/injury |
442	| **Facial** | Geometric landmarks | >90% with ML; FAR ~1 in 1M | <1 s both | $90–$1500 | Vulnerable to spoofing; racial accuracy bias |
443	| **Gait (behavioural)** | Posture/movement | ~99.3% with AI | Continuous | High | Changes with weight/injury |
444	| **Keystroke dynamics** | Typing timing | Moderate | Low overhead | Low | Subtle; changes with fatigue |
445	
446	> [!warning] Bias in Facial Recognition
447	> Facial recognition false-positive rates for Asian and Black individuals can be up to **100× higher** than for white individuals — a significant fairness and reliability concern.
448	
449	### Authorisation Models
450	
451	```mermaid
452	flowchart LR
453	    S["Subject\n(authenticated user)"] --> RM["Reference Monitor\n(policy enforcement)"]
454	    RM --> O["Object\n(file / system / resource)"]
455	```
456	
457	| Model | Who sets access rules | Mechanism | Security level |
458	|-------|----------------------|-----------|----------------|
459	| **DAC** (Discretionary) | **Resource owner** | ACLs + capability tables; Owner/Group/Other categories | Lowest |
460	| **RBAC** (Role-Based) | **System administrator** (by role) | Roles assigned to users; Principle of Least Privilege | Medium — watch for **Role Creep** |
461	| **MAC** (Mandatory) | **OS** (via security labels) | Classification (Top Secret→Unclassified) + Category (need-to-know) | **Highest** — most overhead |
462	
463	#### Role Creep (RBAC Pitfall)
464	A user transfers to a new role but retains their old role's access rights. Requires ongoing role review to prevent privilege accumulation.
465	
466	### Cross-Cutting Controls
467	
468	**Principle of Least Privilege (POLP):** grant only the minimum permissions needed for a task. Limits blast radius of a compromise.
469	
470	**Separation of Duties (SoD):** divide a sensitive task across ≥2 people so no one individual controls it end-to-end.
471	Example: the person who *authorises* a paycheck ≠ the person who *prepares* it.
472	
473	---
474	
475	## §7 — Ethical Hacking
476	
477	### The Defining Line
478	
479	> [!danger] Most Important Concept in This Section
480	> The difference between ethical hacking and a criminal offence is a single word: **authorisation**. The Singapore Computer Misuse Act criminalises *unauthorised* access — the techniques themselves are identical.
481	
482	### Legal Framework
483	
484	**Singapore Computer Misuse Act (CMA / Computer Misuse and Cybersecurity Act, Chapter 50A):**
485	
486	Key offences — all share the word **"unauthorised"**:
487	- Unauthorised access to computer material
488	- Access with intent to commit an offence
489	- Unauthorised modification of computer material
490	- Unauthorised use or interception of a computer service
491	- Unauthorised obstruction of use of a computer
492	- Unauthorised disclosure of an access code
493	
494	**International dimension:** laws vary by country; an act legal in one country may be prosecutable in another (e.g. ILOVEYOU virus — Philippines had no applicable law at the time). The **Convention on Cybercrime** fosters cross-border law enforcement cooperation covering CIA offences, copyright, fraud, and content offences.
495	
496	### Hacker Types
497	
498	| Hat | Authorised? | Description |
499	|-----|------------|-------------|
500	| **White Hat** ✅ | Yes | Security professional; finds and reports vulnerabilities; operates entirely within scope |
501	| **Black Hat** ❌ | No | Malicious; steals, damages, disrupts; purely illegal |
502	| **Gray Hat** ⚠️ | Partially | May have initial authorisation but crosses ethical/legal lines (e.g. selling vulnerability to a competitor; public disclosure after being ignored) |
503	
504	> **Insider threats** (disgruntled employees) are often considered a *greater* organisational risk than external black hats — they already have access.
505	
506	**Key distinction between White and Gray:** White Hat has and *maintains* integrity within scope. Gray Hat has crossed a boundary, leaving them legally exposed.
507	
508	### Pen Testing Approaches
509	
510	| | **Black Box** | **White Box** |
511	|---|---|---|
512	| Prior knowledge | Minimal | Full system knowledge |
513	| Scope | May include social engineering employees | Tests all known aspects |
514	| Style | Covert — mimics a real attacker | Overt — systematic, thorough |
515	
516	### The 6-Stage Hacking Process
517	
518	```mermaid
519	flowchart LR
520	    R["1 Reconnaissance\nInformation Gathering"]
521	    --> S["2 Scanning\nSecurity Posture"]
522	    --> E["3 Enumeration\nServices, Accounts"]
523	    --> G["4 Gaining Access\nExploit Vulnerabilities"]
524	    --> M["5 Maintaining Access\nPersistence, Lateral Move"]
525	    --> C["6 Covering Tracks\nCleanup (ethical) / Evasion"]
526	```
527	
528	#### Stage 1 — Reconnaissance
529	
530	Goal: gather information about the target before touching it.
531	
532	| Technique | Description |
533	|-----------|-------------|
534	| **Shoulder surfing** | Observe directly to capture credentials |
535	| **Dumpster diving** | Search discarded materials for sensitive data |
536	| **Social engineering** | Manipulate people into divulging information |
537	| **Whois** | Reveals domain owner, name servers, admin contacts |
538	| **Google Dorking** | Use search operators to find exposed data passively |
539	| **OSINT tools** | Maltego, Pipl, KnowEm, Netcraft Site Report |
540	
541	**Google Dork examples:**
542	```
543	site:target.com              → limit results to that domain
544	inurl:admin/login.php        → find admin login pages
545	ext:csv inurl:passwd         → find exposed credential files
546	filetype:pdf confidential    → find sensitive PDFs
547	```
548	
549	**Passive vs Active recon:**
550	- **Passive** — no packets sent to target; low detection risk (Google dorking, Whois)
551	- **Active** — direct interaction; target may log your activity; must be authorised
552	
553	#### Stage 2 — Scanning
554	
555	Move from IP addresses (obtained via recon) to identifying **open ports and running services**.
556	
557	| Tool/Technique | What it does |
558	|----------------|-------------|
559	| **Ping** | Checks if a host is alive (ICMP) |
560	| **Ping Sweep (Zenmap / Angry IP)** | Discovers all live hosts in a range |
561	| **Nmap / Zenmap** | Port scan (TCP connect, SYN scan); identifies services |
562	| **Traceroute** (`tracert`) | Maps hops; reveals neighbouring systems for lateral movement |
563	| **Banner Grabbing** | Connects to open port; reads service name/version for exploit selection |
564	| **Nessus** | Automated vulnerability scanner |
565	| **NSE (Nmap Scripting Engine)** | Verifies findings; automates pen testing techniques |
566	
567	**Vulnerability databases:**
568	- `cve.mitre.org` — CVE identifiers for known vulnerabilities
569	- `nvd.nist.gov` — National Vulnerability Database
570	- `exploit-db.com` — Exploit Database (ready-to-use exploits)
571	
572	#### Vulnerability Scanning vs Penetration Testing
573	
574	| | Vulnerability Scanning | Penetration Testing |
575	|---|---|---|
576	| Action | Identifies *potential* weaknesses | Actively **exploits** them for proof |
577	
578	#### Stage 3 — Gaining Access (Exploitation)
579	
580	- Use findings from scanning to select an appropriate exploit
581	- Tools: **Metasploit**, **Kali Linux**, **Hydra**, **Wireshark**, **Cain & Abel**
582	- Classic example: **EternalBlue (MS17-010)** exploit via Metasploit
583	
584	Exploit + Payload model:
585	- **Exploit** — code launched against the vulnerable target
586	- **Payload** — what runs once the exploit succeeds (e.g. reverse shell, RAT)
587	
588	#### Stage 4 — Maintaining Access (Post-Exploitation)
589	
590	| Technique | How it works |
591	|-----------|-------------|
592	| **Create hidden user accounts** | Elevate privileges; hide account from standard listings |
593	| **Modify startup services** | Add malicious scripts to cron / Windows Registry startup |
594	| **Backdoor / RAT** | E.g. **Netcat** — opens a persistent listener; **ProRAT** |
595	| **Rootkit** | Kernel-level malware; deep control; hard to detect |
596	| **Hide files** | `attrib +s +a +h <file>` (Windows CMD); Explorer folder options |
597	
598	#### Stage 5 — Covering Tracks
599	
600	- **For a black hat:** erase logs, hide presence, evade detection
601	- **For a white hat (ethical hacker):** **restore the target machine** — remove installed tools/accounts/backdoors; clean logs of test activity; confirm system is in its original state
602	
603	#### The Pentest Report
604	
605	A professional engagement concludes with a report delivered to an **authorised officer** of the client:
606	- Scope and objectives
607	- Record of findings
608	- Specific remediation advice per vulnerability
609	- Steps for the client going forward
610	
611	> The report — combined with prior authorisation — is what makes ethical hacking demonstrably different from criminal intrusion. The techniques are identical; the paperwork is not.
612	
613	---
614	
615	## §8 — Quick-Reference Summary Tables
616	
617	### Cryptography Decision Matrix
618	
619	| I need to… | Use | Why |
620	|-----------|-----|-----|
621	| Keep data confidential (symmetric) | AES-256 | Fast, current standard |
622	| Agree on a key over insecure channel | Diffie–Hellman | No key transmitted |
623	| Encrypt for one recipient's eyes only | Recipient's **public** key (RSA/asym) | Only they can decrypt |
624	| Sign a document (prove it came from me) | My **private** key | Anyone can verify with my public key |
625	| Verify integrity of data | SHA-256 hash | One-way, collision-resistant |
626	| Sign + encrypt (auth + confidentiality) | Private key → then recipient's public key | Two-pass |
627	
628	### Access Control Model Selector
629	
630	| Situation | Use |
631	|-----------|-----|
632	| User owns the data and should control access | **DAC** |
633	| Organisation-wide role structure; least privilege matters | **RBAC** (but monitor for role creep) |
634	| Government/military; strict need-to-know, classification labels | **MAC** |
635	
636	### Hacker Hat Quick-Check
637	
638	| Scenario | Hat |
639	|----------|-----|
640	| Engaged by Company X; reports vulnerability only to Company X | ⚪ White |
641	| Engaged by Company Y; also sells vulnerability to competitor | 🩶 Gray |
642	| Exploits Company X's vulnerability; installs malware | ⚫ Black |
643	| Engaged by Company Y; report ignored; posts publicly | 🩶 Gray |
644	| Disgruntled employee; insider access | ⚫ Black (insider threat) |
645	
646	---
647	
648	## §9 — Common Exam Mistakes
649	
650	> [!warning] Common Mistakes — Memorise These
651	
652	1. **Transposition ciphers are NOT immune to frequency analysis** — they rearrange positions but preserve character frequencies.
653	2. **DH is not encryption** — it establishes a shared key; encryption is a separate step.
654	3. **RSA key generation uses `φ(n)` not `n`** — encryption/decryption use `n`; the generation step uses `(p−1)(q−1)`.
655	4. **Hashing alone ≠ digital signature** — a signature additionally encrypts the hash with the sender's private key.
656	5. **MD5 and SHA-1 are broken** — do not cite them as "secure hash algorithms."
657	6. **Salt defeats rainbow tables; encryption does NOT** — only the one-way + salt combination is truly robust.
658	7. **LSB steganography fails on JPEG** — lossy compression destroys embedded bits. PNG/TIFF/BMP only.
659	8. **Authentication ≠ Authorisation** — authentication proves identity; authorisation determines what that identity may do.
660	9. **RBAC Role Creep** — always mention the need for ongoing role review when writing about RBAC.
661	10. **Ethical hacking requires *legal authorisation*, not just good intentions** — intentions alone never make it legal.

## ICT3112 — Software Verification and Validation

### Cyclomatic Complexity

Cyclomatic complexity, introduced by Thomas McCabe in 1976, gives you a single number that represents the minimum number of independent paths through a module — and therefore the minimum number of test cases needed to guarantee at least branch coverage.

**Formula:**

$$C = E - N + 2$$

where **E** is the number of edges in the Control Flow Graph (CFG) and **N** is the number of nodes.

**Worked Example — Factorial Function:**
The factorial CFG has 12 edges and 11 nodes, so:

$$C = 12 - 11 + 2 = 3$$

This means there are three independent (basis) paths, and you need at least three test cases:
- Path 1: `num < 0` → prints "nope"
- Path 2: `num = 0` → loop is skipped entirely
- Path 3: `num > 0` → loop runs at least once

**Why it matters for exams:** The complexity value tells you *both* the test case count *and* the risk level of the code.

| C Range | Risk Assessment |
|---------|----------------|
| 1–4 | Simple, low risk |
| 5–10 | Marginal, low risk |
| 11–20 | Moderate risk |
| 21–50 | High risk |
| > 50 | Untestable, very high risk |

> [!warning] Watch Out
> The back-edge in a loop (e.g. node 9 → node 6 in the factorial example) **is an edge and must be counted**. Students who forget the back-edge will under-count E by one and compute C = 2 instead of 3. Always trace every arrow in the CFG, including those pointing backwards.

**Memory hook:** "Edges minus Nodes plus 2 = paths to pursue."

### Decision / Branch Coverage

Decision coverage (also called branch coverage) requires every **decision outcome** — both the True branch and the False branch of every `if`, `while`, `for`, or `switch` statement — to be executed at least once. It is stronger than statement coverage because it is possible to achieve 100% statement coverage while leaving one branch of a decision untested.

**Formula:**

$$\text{Coverage \%} = \frac{\text{decision outcomes executed}}{\text{total decision outcomes}} \times 100$$

**Worked Example:**
Consider code with two decisions: an `if (num < 0)` and a `while (i <= num)`. Each decision has a True and a False outcome → 4 outcomes in total.

| Test Case | Input | if → True/False | while → True/False |
|-----------|-------|-----------------|-------------------|
| TC1 | num = −1 | **True** ✓ | **False** ✓ (loop skipped) |
| TC2 | num = 3 | **False** ✓ | **True** ✓ (loop runs) |

Two test cases cover all four decision outcomes → 100% decision coverage.

**Key property:** Decision coverage **subsumes** statement coverage — achieving decision coverage automatically gives you statement coverage. The reverse is not true.

> [!warning] Watch Out
> Do not confuse decision coverage with condition coverage. Decision coverage asks "did both outcomes of the entire decision fire?" Condition coverage asks "did each individual sub-condition take both True and False?" — and critically, condition coverage does **not** subsume decision coverage. It is entirely possible to achieve 100% condition coverage while never executing one branch of a compound decision. This distinction is a favourite exam question.

**Memory hook:** "Decision coverage = both branches walked; condition coverage = each sub-flag flipped."

### Equivalence Partitioning

Equivalence partitioning (EP) is a blackbox technique designed to minimise the number of test cases whilst maintaining broad input coverage. The fundamental insight is that if the system behaves identically for all values within a group (a *partition*), testing one representative value from that group tells you just as much as testing them all.

**Mechanism:**
1. Divide the input domain into partitions where every value produces the same result.
2. Identify both **valid** and **invalid** partitions — both must be tested.
3. Select **one representative value** from each partition.

**Worked Example — Integer input, valid range 0–100:**

```
◄──────────────────────────────────────►
   Invalid 1   |      Valid       | Invalid 2
    x < 0      |   0 ≤ x ≤ 100   |  x > 100
───────────────────────────────────────────
    e.g. −10          e.g. 50       e.g. 110
```

Minimum test set: **3 test cases** (one per partition). You do not need to test −9, −8, −7 … because they all represent the same invalid case.

EP can also be applied to **output** partitions, not only inputs.

> [!warning] Watch Out
> A very common mistake is to omit the invalid partitions entirely, testing only the valid range. Exam questions often ask for the "complete minimum test set" — this always includes representatives from invalid partitions as well. A test set that only tests valid inputs is incomplete by definition.

**Memory hook:** "One per partition — valid and invalid both count."

## ICT3113 — Performance Optimisation and Design

### Little's Law and the M/M/1 Queue

**Little's Law** is the single most important result in queueing theory. It states:

$$N = X \times R$$

where **N** is the average number of items in the system, **X** is the throughput (completions per unit time), and **R** is the average time each item spends in the system (response time). It holds for any stable system, regardless of arrival distribution, service distribution, or number of servers.

You can also apply it to the queue alone:

$$N_{queue} = X \times W$$

where **W** is the wait time (time spent in queue before service begins).

**Worked Example:**
An API server processes requests at a throughput of 10 requests per second. Each request spends an average of 0.4 seconds in the system. How many requests are in the system on average?

$$N = 10 \times 0.4 = 4 \text{ requests}$$

**The M/M/1 Queue** is the simplest analytical model: Markov (Poisson) arrivals at rate λ, Markov (exponential) service at rate μ, single server. The stability condition is ρ = λ/μ < 1.

Key results:

| Metric | Formula |
|--------|---------|
| Traffic intensity | ρ = λ/μ = λ × S |
| Wait in queue | W = ρ/(1−ρ) × S |
| Response time | R = S / (1−ρ) |

As ρ approaches 1, R grows without bound — the system becomes unstable and queues form indefinitely. This is why real systems are deliberately run below 70–80% utilisation: the relationship between utilisation and response time is highly non-linear, and small increases in load near saturation cause disproportionately large increases in wait time.

> [!warning] Watch Out
> In a short finite observation window, the mean of observed inter-arrival gaps does **not** equal 1/λ. Always compute λ as (number of arrivals) ÷ (total window length). Dividing by the mean gap will give you the wrong answer. This distinction is explicitly tested in exams.

**Memory hook:** "N = XR — jobs in system equals rate times residence."

### The Kingman Formula

Whilst the M/M/1 model assumes both arrivals and service times follow exponential distributions (coefficient of variation = 1 for both), real systems have variable service times — mixed workloads, long reports alongside fast lookups, bursty arrival patterns. The **Kingman formula** quantifies how variability inflates wait time:

$$W \approx \underbrace{\frac{\rho}{1-\rho}}_{\text{utilisation term}} \times \underbrace{\frac{C_a^2 + C_s^2}{2}}_{\text{variability term}} \times \underbrace{S}_{\text{service time}}$$

- **ρ/(1−ρ)** is the same utilisation-driven term as M/M/1
- **(Cₐ² + Cₛ²)/2** scales the wait up or down depending on variability
- **Cₐ** = coefficient of variation of inter-arrival times; **Cₛ** = coefficient of variation of service times
- When Cₐ = Cₛ = 1 (both exponential), the formula reduces exactly to the M/M/1 result

**Worked Example (ρ = 0.8, S = 100 ms):**

| Scenario | Cₐ² | Cₛ² | Variability term | W |
|----------|-----|-----|-----------------|---|
| Deterministic (regular) | 0 | 0 | 0 | ≈ 0 ms |
| M/M/1 (Poisson/Exp) | 1 | 1 | 1 | 4 × 1 × 100 = **400 ms** |
| Mixed workload | 1 | 4 | 2.5 | 4 × 2.5 × 100 = **1,000 ms** |

The utilisation term at ρ = 0.8 is 0.8/0.2 = **4**. The mixed workload has 2.5× the wait of M/M/1 — with *identical* hardware, load, and mean service time. The extra 600 ms comes purely from variance.

**Practical implication:** If your system shows high tail latency at moderate utilisation, variability — not capacity — is almost certainly the root cause. The fix is to separate heavy and light workloads into distinct queues to reduce Cₛ.

> [!warning] Watch Out
> Kingman applies to a **single server (G/G/1)**. For multiple servers, use Sakasegawa's approximation (which modifies the utilisation term). Do not apply the G/G/1 formula directly to a multi-server system.

**Memory hook:** "Kingman = utilisation × variability × service time — all three must be tamed."

## INF2005 — Cyber Security Fundamentals

### RSA Key Generation

RSA is an asymmetric encryption algorithm whose security rests on the practical impossibility of factoring the product of two large prime numbers. You must know the six-step key generation procedure for the exam.

**Six Steps:**

1. Pick two large distinct primes, **p** and **q**
2. Compute the modulus: **n = p × q**
3. Compute Euler's totient: **φ(n) = (p−1)(q−1)**
4. Choose public exponent **e** such that 1 < e < φ(n) and gcd(e, φ(n)) = 1 (i.e. e and φ(n) are coprime)
5. Compute private exponent **d** such that **d × e ≡ 1 mod φ(n)** (i.e. d is the modular multiplicative inverse of e)
6. **Public key = (e, n)** · **Private key = (d, n)**

**Encryption and Decryption:**
- Encrypt: C = Mᵉ mod n
- Decrypt: M = Cᵈ mod n

**Worked Example (small primes for illustration):**
- p = 5, q = 11 → n = 55, φ(n) = 4 × 10 = 40
- Choose e = 3 (gcd(3, 40) = 1 ✓)
- Find d: 3d ≡ 1 mod 40 → d = 27 (since 3 × 27 = 81 = 2×40 + 1)
- Public key = (3, 55) · Private key = (27, 55)

**Why it is secure:** An attacker knows e and n (both public), but cannot compute d without knowing φ(n), which in turn requires factoring n back into p and q — computationally infeasible for large n.

> [!warning] Watch Out
> Key generation uses modulus **φ(n)** — not n. Encryption and decryption use modulus **n** — not φ(n). These are different values. Mixing them up in an exam answer will cost marks. Also remember: the RSA private key is (d, n), **not** just d.

**Memory hook:** "Generation uses φ(n); encryption uses n — phi for private-key craft, n for message transform."

### LSB Steganography

Steganography hides the *existence* of a message, whereas cryptography hides its *content*. LSB (Least Significant Bit) steganography exploits the fact that altering only the rightmost bit of a pixel byte causes a value change of at most 1 out of 255 — visually imperceptible to the human eye.

**Core idea:** Replace (or adjust) the LSB of each pixel byte with one bit of the secret payload. A 1024×1024 RGB image has 3,145,728 pixel channels, giving a raw capacity of ~393 KB of hidden data.

**Two Variants:**

| Variant | How it works | Detectability |
|---------|-------------|---------------|
| **LSB Replacement** | Directly set the LSB to the payload bit | Higher — creates statistical asymmetry in pixel-value distribution |
| **LSB Matching** | If LSB ≠ payload bit, randomly add or subtract 1 from the pixel value | Lower — avoids the detectable hard-flip pattern |

LSB Matching is more resistant to statistical steganalysis because it avoids the signature left by pure replacement.

**Critical format constraint:** LSB steganography works only in **lossless image formats** — PNG, TIFF, BMP. JPEG uses lossy compression, which discards small bit-level changes during encoding, destroying any embedded payload.

**Bit plane insight:** Every colour channel can be decomposed into 8 bit planes (bit 0 = LSB, bit 7 = MSB). The LSB plane (bit 0) naturally resembles random noise even in unmodified images, which explains why embedding data there is visually imperceptible.

**Steganalysis:** To detect LSB Replacement, apply a visual attack — map even pixel values to black and odd pixel values to white. Hidden messages create structured patterns in this view, whereas a clean image appears as true random noise.

> [!warning] Watch Out
> JPEG will destroy your hidden data. Students regularly confuse image formats in exam questions. PNG is lossless and safe for LSB; JPEG is lossy and will corrupt the payload. Also note: LSB Replacement changes approximately 50% of LSBs on average (not 100%), because half the cover pixels already carry the correct bit value.

**Memory hook:** "LSB lives in lossless — PNG yes, JPEG no."
